The Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published in April 2025 by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), is the eighth edition of the report. This edition is the most comprehensive to date, incorporating in-depth analyses of AI hardware, estimates of inference costs, and analyses of AI publication and patenting trends. It also provides data on corporate adoption of responsible AI (RAI) practices and expanded coverage of AI's role in science and medicine. The AI Index was founded in 2017 as an offshoot of the One Hundred Year Study of Artificial Intelligence (AI100) to provide policymakers, journalists, executives, researchers, and the public with rigorously validated, globally sourced data. 

### Administration and Production

The report was produced by the AI Index Steering Committee, including Chair Raymond Perrault and Chair-elect Jack Clark, and an editorial team led by Research Manager and Editor-in-Chief Nestor Maslej. The writing process was aided by AI tools, specifically ChatGPT and Claude, which were used to tighten and copy edit initial drafts written by human researchers. Feedback and new ideas for future editions are welcome via Nestor Maslej (nmaslej@stanford.edu). Raw data and charts are available on Google Drive, and the Global AI Vibrancy Tool, which allows for the comparison of AI ecosystems across over 30 countries, will be updated in the summer of 2025.

### Overview and Global Trends

Co-directors Yolanda Gil and Raymond Perrault state that 2024 was a pivotal year. AI's role in advancing knowledge was recognized by Nobel prizes in physics and chemistry, and the Turing award for reinforcement learning. The Turing Test is no longer considered an ambitious goal as sophisticated systems have surpassed it. Corporate investment rebounded in 2024, with the number of newly funded generative AI startups nearly tripling, and business adoption of AI accelerated significantly.

Governments have increased their involvement, launching billion-dollar national AI infrastructure initiatives, including expanding energy capacity. However, public trust remains a challenge. While a 2024 global survey showed a rise in optimism about AI's societal benefits, fewer people believe AI companies safeguard data, and concerns regarding fairness and bias persist.

### Chapter 1: Research and Development

Industry now dominates notable AI model development, with nearly 90% of such models in 2024 originating from industry, compared to 60% in 2023. Conversely, academia remains the leading producer of highly cited (top 100) publications. China leads in total AI publications (23.2% in 2023) and citations (22.6% in 2023), while the United States leads in highly influential research and remains the primary source of notable AI models, producing 40 in 2024 compared to China's 15 and Europe's combined total of three. In the past decade, the U.S. has produced more notable machine learning models than any other country.

Between 2013 and 2023, AI publications in computer science and other scientific disciplines nearly tripled, rising from approximately 102,000 to over 242,000. AI's share of computer science publications increased from 21.6% in 2013 to 41.8% in 2023. AI patenting is also increasing; from 2010 to 2023, AI patents grew from 3,833 to 122,511, with a 29.6% increase in the last year. China leads in total AI patents, accounting for 69.7% of all grants as of 2023. South Korea and Luxembourg are the top producers on a per capita basis.

Regarding model development, training compute for notable AI models doubles every five months, dataset sizes for LLMs double every eight months, and the power required for training doubles annually. In terms of costs, the inference cost for a system performing at the level of GPT-3.5 (64.8 on MMLU) dropped from $20.00 per million tokens in November 2022 to $0.07 per million tokens by October 2024 (Gemini-1.5-Flash-8B), a more than 280-fold reduction. LLM inference prices have fallen between 9 and 900 times per year depending on the task.

AI hardware performance (measured in 16-bit floating-point operations) has grown 43% annually, doubling every 1.9 years. Costs have dropped 30% per year, and energy efficiency has increased by 40% annually. However, carbon emissions from training have risen sharply. Training AlexNet (2012) emitted 0.01 tons of carbon, GPT-3 (2020) emitted 588 tons, GPT-4 (2023) emitted 5,184 tons, and Llama 3.1 405B (2024) emitted 8,930 tons. For comparison, the average American emits 18 tons of carbon per year.

### Chapter 2: Technical Performance

AI systems are mastering benchmarks faster than ever. In 2024, scores on MMMU, GPQA, and SWE-bench rose by 18.8, 48.9, and 67.3 percentage points, respectively, compared to 2023. On SWE-bench specifically, AI systems improved from solving 4.4% of coding problems in 2023 to 71.7% in 2024. 

Open-weight models are rapidly closing the gap with closed-weight models. In early January 2024, the leading closed-weight model outperformed the top open-weight model by 8.0% on the Chatbot Arena Leaderboard; by February 2025, this gap narrowed to 1.7%.

Similarly, the performance gap between Chinese and U.S. models is narrowing. At the end of 2023, gaps on MMLU, MMMU, MATH, and HumanEval were 17.5, 13.5, 24.3, and 31.6 percentage points, respectively. By the end of 2024, these margins shrunk to 0.3, 8.1, 1.6, and 3.7 percentage points.

Frontier model performance is converging. The Elo score difference between the top and 10th-ranked model on the Chatbot Arena Leaderboard fell from 11.9% to 5.4% in a year. The difference between the top two models shrank from 4.9% in 2023 to 0.7% in 2024.

New reasoning paradigms, such as test-time compute (e.g., OpenAI's o1 and o3 models), improve performance. The o1 model scored 74.4% on an International Mathematical Olympiad qualifying exam, compared to 9.3% for GPT-4o. However, o1 is nearly six times more expensive and 30 times slower than GPT-4o.

Due to the saturation of traditional benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval), new, more challenging evaluations are emerging. These include Humanity’s Last Exam (top system scores 8.80%), FrontierMath (AI solves only 2%), and BigCodeBench (AI systems achieve 35.5% success vs. human standard of 97%).

High-quality AI video generation saw significant gains in 2024 with the launch of SORA, Stable Video Diffusion 3D and 4D, Movie Gen, and Veo 2. Video generation and programming tasks are also areas of significant stride.

Performance gains are also being seen in smaller models. In 2022, the smallest model scoring over 60% on MMLU was PaLM (540 billion parameters). By 2024, Microsoft’s Phi-3-mini (3.8 billion parameters) achieved this, a 142-fold reduction in size.

Despite these advances, complex reasoning remains a challenge. LLMs still struggle with benchmarks like PlanBench and frequently fail logic tasks where correct solutions exist, even with chain-of-thought reasoning.

AI agents are showing early promise; in short time-horizon settings (two-hour budget), top systems score four times higher than human experts according to RE-Bench. However, in 32-hour budget settings, human performance surpasses AI two to one.

### Chapter 3: Responsible AI (RAI)

Evaluation of AI systems using RAI criteria remains uncommon, though new benchmarks like HELM Safety, AIR-Bench, and FACTS are emerging to assess factuality and safety. Other factuality benchmarks include the updated Hughes Hallucination Evaluation Model leaderboard, SimpleQA, and the previous HaluEval and TruthfulQA.

AI-related incidents are rising. The AI Incidents Database reports that incidents rose to 233 in 2024, a 56.4% increase over 2023. Organizations acknowledge RAI risks, but mitigation efforts lag. A McKinsey survey shows top concerns are inaccuracy (64%), regulatory compliance (63%), and cybersecurity (60%), but not all are taking active steps.

Policymakers are increasingly involved. In 2024, the OECD, European Union, United Nations, and African Union published frameworks for the transparency, explainability, and and trustworthiness of AI.

Transparency in foundation model research is improving, as shown by the Foundation Model Transparency Index, where average scores for major developers increased from 37% in October 2023 to 58% in May 2024.

However, the "data commons" is shrinking. In the C4 common crawl dataset, the proportion of restricted tokens jumped from 5–7% to 20–33% between 2023 and 2024 as websites implement protocols to curb data scraping.

AI-related election misinformation spread globally in 2024 across more than a dozen countries and over 10 social media platforms, including the U.S. presidential election.

Implicit bias remains a problem. Models such as GPT-4 and Claude 3 Sonnet continue to associate negative terms with Black individuals, associate women with humanities rather than STEM, and favor men for leadership roles.

Academic research into RAI is growing, with the number of RAI papers accepted at leading conferences increasing by 28.8% (from 992 in 2023 to 1,278 in 2024).

### Chapter 4: Economy

Global private AI investment reached a record $252.3 billion in 2024, a 26% increase. Private investment grew 44.5% and mergers and acquisitions (M&A) rose 12.1% from the previous year. Total investment has grown more than thirteenfold since 2014.

Generative AI specifically attracted $33.9 billion in global private investment in 2024, an 18.7% increase from 2023. Generative AI now represents more than 20% of all AI-related private investment.

The United States leads significantly in private investment. In 2024, U.S. private AI investment reached $109.1 billion, nearly 12 times that of China ($9.3 billion) and 24 times that of the U.K. ($4.5 billion). In generative AI, the U.S. investment gap exceeded the combined total of China, the EU, and the U.K. by $25.4 billion in 2024, expanding from a $21.8 billion gap in 2023.

Organizational use of AI has surged. In 2024, 78% of organizations reported using AI, up from 55% in 2023. Use of generative AI in at least one business function rose from 33% in 2024 to 71% in 2024. 

AI is beginning to deliver financial impact. Among companies reporting financial impacts, 49% of those using AI in service operations, 43% in supply chain management, and 4 the 41% in software engineering report cost savings (though most report these savings are less than 10%). Regarding revenue, 71% of those using AI in marketing and sales, 63% in supply chain management, and 57% in service operations report revenue gains (though most report these increases are less than 5%).

Regional shifts in AI use are evident. While North America leads, Greater China saw one of the most significant growth rates, with a 27 percentage point increase. Europe followed with a 23 percentage point increase.

China continues to dominate industrial robotics. In 2023, China installed 276,300 industrial robots, 6 times more than Japan and 7.3 times more than the United States. China's share of global installations has risen to 51.1% since 2013. Collaborative and interactive robot installations are increasing; collaborative robots grew from 2.8% of all new installations in 2017 to 10.5% by 2023. Service robot installations also rose in 2023 across all categories except medical robotics.

AI's energy demands are driving interest in nuclear energy. Microsoft has a $1.6 billion deal to revive the Three Mile Island nuclear reactor, and Google and Amazon have also secured nuclear energy agreements.

### Chapter 5: Science and Medicine

In 2024, high-performance protein sequencing models like ESM3 and AlphaFold 3 were launched. AI continues to drive scientific discovery through tools like Aviary (biological tasks) and FireSat (wildfire prediction). 

Clinical knowledge in LLMs is improving. OpenAI's o1 model achieved 96.0% on the MedQA benchmark, a 5.8 percentage point gain over the best 2023 score. Performance on MedQA has improved by 28.4 percentage points since late 2022. 

AI has shown the ability to outperform doctors in specific clinical tasks, such as diagnosing complex clinical cases (GPT-4), cancer detection, and identifying high-mortality-risk patients. However, the best results are often achieved through AI-doctor collaboration.

FDA-approved, AI-enabled medical devices increased from six in 2015 to 223 by 2023. 

Synthetic data is showing promise in medicine for identifying social determinants of health, discovering new drug compounds, and enhancing privacy-preserving clinical risk prediction.

Medical foundation models were released in 2024, including multimodal models like Med-Gemini and specialized models for echocardiology (EchoCLIP), ophthalmology (VisionFM), and radiology (ChexAgent).

Public protein science databases have grown significantly since 2021, with entries increasing in AlphaFold (585%), Pcorresponding to PDB (23%) and UniProt (31%).

AI-driven research earned two Nobel Prizes in 2024: Demis Hassabis and John Jumper (Google DeepMind) for protein folding with AlphaFold (Chemistry), and John Hopfield and and Geoffrey Hinton for neural networks (Physics).

### Chapter 6: Policy and Governance

U.S. states are leading AI legislation due to slow federal progress. State-level AI laws increased from one in 2016 to 49 by 2023, and 131 by 2024. U.S. federal agencies introduced 59 AI-related regulations in 2024, more than double the 25 regulations from 21 agencies in 2023. 

Global governments are investing in AI infrastructure. Major investments include: 
- Canada: $2.4 billion
- China: $47.5 billion semiconductor fund
- China: $47.5 billion semiconductor fund
- France: €109 billion (committed) / $117 billion (mentioned)
- India: $1.25 billion
- Saudi Arabia: $100 billion (Project Transcendence)

Mentions of AI in legislative proceedings across 75 countries increased by 21.3% in 2024, rising from 1,557 to 1,889. Since 2016, total mentions have grown more than ninefold.

International AI safety institutes were launched in 2024. Following the the AI Seoul Summit in May 2024, institutes were pledged in Japan, France, Germany, Italy, Singapore, South Korea, Australia, Canada, and the EU, following the initial U.S. and U.K. institutes (Nov 2023).

U.S. states have expanded deepfake regulations. By 2024, 24 states had passed regulations, with 15 more (including New York, Oregon, and New Mexico) introducing measures in 2024.

### Chapter 7: Education

In the U.S., 81% of high school CS teachers agree that AI should be part of the foundational CS experience, but fewer than half feel equipped to teach it. 

Global access to K–12 CS education has expanded, with two-thirds of countries now offering or plan to offer it, doubling since 2019. 

In the U.S., the number of graduates earning master's degrees in the field of AI nearly doubled between 2022 and 2023. 

The United States is the global leader in producing ICT (information, technology, and communications) graduates, followed by Spain, Brazil, and the United Kingdom.

### Chapter 8: Public Opinion

Global optimism about AI has risen, with 55% of people seeing it as more beneficial than harmful as of 2024, up from 52% in 2022. In 18 of 26 nations surveyed by Ipsos, optimism increased. 

Two-thirds of people globally believe AI-powered products and services will significantly impact daily life within the next three to five years. The largest jumps in perception were in Canada (+17%) and Germany (+15%).

However, trust in AI companies is declining. Global confidence that AI companies protect personal data fell from 50% in 2023 to 47% in 2024. Confidence that AI systems are unbiased and free from discrimination is also falling.

Regional differences in optimism remain stark. Majorities in China (83%), Indonesia (80%), and Thailand (77%) view AI as beneficial. In contrast, minorities in Canada (40%), United States (39%), and the Netherlands (36%) view it as beneficial. 

In the U.S., 61% of people fear self-driving cars, and only 13% trust them (American Automobile Association survey).

Local U.S. policymakers support AI regulation. In 2023, 73.7% of the local policymakers agreed that AI should be regulated, up from 55.7% in 2022. Support for regulation is stronger among Democrats (79.2%) versus Republicans (55.5%).

Countries previously most skeptical of AI showed the sharpest gains in optimism from 2022 to 2024: Germany (+10%), France (+10%), Canada (+8%), Great Britain (+8%), and the United States (+4%).

Regarding the workforce, 60% of respondents agree AI will change how they do their jobs in the next five years, and 36% believe it will replace their jobs. People expect AI to save time (55%) and offer better entertainment (51%), but are less confident in its impact on health (38%), the national economy (36%), and the job market (31%).

Local U.S. policymakers' specific priorities for regulation vary. There is strong support for stricter data privacy rules (80.4%), retraining for the unemployed (76.2%), and AI deployment regulations (72.5%). There is low support for a law enforcement facial recognition ban (34.2%), wage subsidies for wage declines (32.9%), and universal basic income (24.6%).

### Final Report Details

The report's table of contents includes: Report Highlights (p. 12), Chapter 1: Research and Development (p. 24), Chapter 2: Technical Performance (p. 24), Chapter 3: Responsible AI (p. 160), Chapter 4: Economy (p. 24), Chapter 5: Science and Medicine (p. 280), Chapter 6: Policy and Governance (p. 323), Chapter 7: Education (p. 7), Chapter 8: Public Opinion (p. 394), and Appendix (p. 414).

(Note: The Table of Contents entries for Technical Performance and Economy are listed as page 24 in the children, but follow Research and Development.)

### Summary

 The Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025 from Stanford HAI provides a comprehensive analysis of AI, noting a record $252.3 billion in global private investment in 2024, a 280-fold reduction in inference costs for GPT-3.5 level models, and a performance convergence at the frontier where the top two models are separated by only 0.7%.

The Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, provides a comprehensive analysis of the global landscape of AI research, patents, and model development. 

### AI Research Output and Influence

AI research is distributed geographically and by sector. In 2023, East Asia and the Pacific led in research output, accounting for 34.5% of all AI publications, followed by Europe and Central Asia at 18.2% and North America at 10.3%. In terms of influence, East Asia and the Pacific held the largest share of citations in 2023 at 37.1%. While North America and East Asia and the Pacific had roughly equal citation shares in 2017, North American and European shares have since declined as East Asia and the Pacific's share has risen sharply.

On a country level, China was the global leader in AI article publications in 2023, accounting for 23.2% of the total. Other leaders included Europe (15.2%), India and the United States (each at 9.2%). Since 2016, China's share of publications has steadily increased, while the U.S. share remained stable until 2021 before slightly declining. In 2023, Chinese AI publications accounted for 22.6% of all citations, followed by Europe at 20.9% and the United States at 13.0%. The late 2010s marked the turning point where China surpassed the U.S. and Europe as the leading source of citations.

By sector, academic institutions remained the primary source of AI publications worldwide in 2023, accounting for 84.9% of all publications, compared to 85.9% in 2013. Industry contributed 7.1% and government institutions 4.9%, while nonprofit organizations contributed 1.7%. Regional differences exist: in the United States, 16.5% of AI publications originate from industry, whereas in China, only 8.0% do. Conversely, China has the highest percentage of AI publications from the education sector at 84.5%.

Research topics in 2023 were dominated by machine learning (75.7%), followed by computer vision (47.2%), pattern recognition (25.9%), and natural language processing (17.1%), with a sharp increase in publications on generative AI.

Analysis of the 100 most-cited AI publications from 2021 to 2023 shows that the United States consistently had the highest number of top-cited publications: 64 in 2021, 59 in 2022, and 50 in 2023, although its share has gradually declined. China ranked second in each of those years. By sector, academia consistently produced the most top-cited research: 34 publications in 2021, 27 in 2022, and 42 in 2023. Industry contributions dropped from 17 in 2021 and 19 in 2022 to 7 in 2023. By organization, Google led each year from 2021 to 2023, tying with Tsinghua University in 2023 when both contributed eight publications to the top 100. In 2023, Carnegie Mellon University was the highest-ranked U.S. academic institution.

### AI Patents and Notable Models

Regarding AI patents, using PATSTAT Global data from the European Patent Office, the number of granted AI patents worldwide grew from 3,833 in 2010 to 122,511 in 2023, with a 29.6% increase in the last year. Regional distribution shows a widening gap: 82.4% of granted AI patents as of 2023 originated from East Asia and the Pacific, with North America at 14.2%. China led globally with 69.7% of all granted patents in 2023, followed by the United States at 14.2%. The U.S. share declined from a peak of 42.8% in 2015.

Per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023, South Korea had the most AI patents with 17.27, followed by Luxembourg (15.31), China (6.08), the United States (5.20), and Japan (4.58). Between 2013 and 2023, Luxembourg (8,216%), China (6,317%), and Sweden (3,453%) saw the greatest percentage increase in per capita patenting.

"Notable machine learning models" are influential models selected by Epoch AI based on state-of-the-art advancements, historical significance, or high citation rates. In 2024, the United States led in the production of notable AI models with 40 models, followed by China with 15 and France with three. All major geographic groups (U.S., China, Europe) released fewer notable models in 2024 than in 2023. Since 2003, the United States has produced more notable models than the UK, China, and Canada.

Industry has led in releasing notable models since 2014. In 2024, industry produced 55 notable AI models, and no notable AI models originated from academia in 2024. The proportion of notable AI models from industry grew to 90.2% in 2024. Over the past decade, Google has led in production with 187 models, followed by Meta (82) and Microsoft (39). In 2024 specifically, top contributors were Google (7 models), OpenAI (7 models), and Alibaba (6 models). Since 2014, the most prolific academic institutions have been Carnegie Mellon University (25), Stanford University (25), and Tsinghua University (22).

### Model Development, Training, and Access

Detailed data on notable AI models from 2014 to 2024 shows that Google produced the most (187), followed by Meta (82), Microsoft (39), OpenAI (36), Carnegie Mellon University (25), Stanford University (25), Tsinghua University (22), UC Berkeley (22), Nvidia (17), the University of Oxford (16), MIT (15), Salesforce (15), the University of Washington (15), Alibaba (14), and the Allen Institute for AI (12). DeepMind research is categorized under Google.

Notable AI models are released under various access types. API access allows interaction via queries without direct weight access; Hosted access (no API) is via platform interface only (e.g., Gemini 2.0 Pro); Open weights (restricted use) provide weights but limit commercial use or redistribution (e.g., DeepSeek-V3); Open weights (unrestricted) allow free use, modification, and redistribution (e.g., AlphaGeometry); Open weights (noncommercial) restrict use to research or noncommercial purposes (e.g.,g Mistral Large 2); and unreleased models remain private (e.g., ESM3 98B). In 2024, API access was the most common release type (20 of 61 models), accounting for 32.8% of notable models. Other 2024 release types included Open weights (restricted use) at 18.03%, Unreleased at 16.39%, Open weights (unrestricted) at 11.48%, Open weights (noncommercial) at 9.84%, Hosted access (no API) at 8.20%, and Unknown at 3.28%.

In 2024, 60.7% of notable AI models were launched without corresponding training code, contrasting with traditional open-source software practices.

Model parameters—numerical values learned during training—have risen sharply since the early 2010s. Training dataset sizes for LLMs double approximately every eight months. For example, the Transformer model (2017) was trained on 2 billion tokens, GPT-3 175B (davinci) on 374 billion tokens, and Meta’s Llama 3.3 (2024) on 15 trillion tokens. Training times have also increased: AlexNet (2012) took five to six days, Llama 3.1-405B took approximately 90 days, and Google’s Gemini 1.0 Ultra (2023) took around 100 days.

Compute refers to the computational resources required to train and operate a model. Training compute for notable AI models doubles roughly every five months. For instance, AlexNet (2012) required 470 petaFLOP, the original Transformer (2017) required 7,400 petaFLOP, and GPT-4o required 38 billion petaFLOP.

### Compute Scaling and Data Bottlenecks

DeepSeek’s V3 model (December 2024) achieved high performance with fewer computational resources than leading LLMs. However, top 10 Chinese language models have scaled their training compute at a rate of approximately three times per year since late 2021, which is slower than the five times per year trend seen globally since 2018. Top-tier U.S. models have generally been more computationally intensive than those from China.

There is a significant debate on whether AI models will run out of training data. Epoch AI estimates the total effective stock of data available for training: Common Crawl contains a median of 130 trillion tokens, the indexed web holds 510 trillion tokens, and the entire web (including private data)andung 3,100 trillion tokens. Image stocks are estimated at 300 trillion and video at 1,350 trillion. Epoch AI projects, with an 80% confidence interval, that the current stock of training data will be fully utilized between 2026 and 2032. 

This projection revises earlier estimates that high-quality text data would be depleted by 2024. The update is based on research showing that web data performs better than curated corpora and that models can be trained on the same datasets multiple times. Concerns exist regarding synthetic data; models trained on repeated cycles of synthetic data likely lose representation of the tails of distributions, leading to "model collapse." However, when synthetic data is layered on top of real data rather than replacing it, collapse does not occur, though it not necessarily improves performance or reduces test loss. 

Synthetic data's high-fidelity generation is improving, though it remains distinguishable from real data. Some methods, such as using Synthetic Data Vault (SDV) versus Walmart data to train an XGBoost classifier, showed synthetic data could outperform real data in some cases. In the healthcare domain, some architectures using synthetic data have shown enhanced performance, increasing F1 scores or AUROC by 5%–10% on minority classes. To improve factuality, the FactTune-FS methods introduced by Stanford and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill have tended to outperform other RLHF and decoding-based methods.

As web content becomes increasingly AI-generated, future models will be trained on non-human material. While synthetic data and data augmentation (modifying real data through tilting or image mixing) and offer a near-infinite supply, their effective use requires further research into learning dynamics.

### Inference Costs and Performance

Inference costs—the expense of querying a trained model, measured in USD per million tokens—have decreased substantially for fixed performance thresholds. For a model scoring the equivalent of GPT-3.5 (64.8 on MMLU), the cost dropped from $20 per million tokens in November 2022 to $0.07 per million tokens in October 2024 (Gemini-1.5-Flash-8B), a more than 280-fold reduction. For models scoring above 50% on GPQA, costs declined from $15 per million tokens in May 2024 to December 2024 (Phi 4) at $0.12 per million tokens. Epoch AI estimates that LLM inference costs have fallen between nine and 900 times per year depending on the task. 

While top-tier models from developers like OpenAI, Meta, and Anthropic remain more expensive, reflecting a premium for the premium performance, the general trend is a clear improvement in AI performance per dollar spent.
block-L0-002.summary: The AI Index Report 2025 reveals a China-led surge in AI research publications (23.2% share) and patents (69.7% share) by 2023, while the U.S. leads in notable AI models (40 in 2024) and top-cited research. The report also highlights a training compute doubling every five months and a massive reduction in inference costs, such as GPT-3.5 level performance costs falling from $20 to $0.07 per million tokens.

block-L0-003.context:
The Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, provides a comprehensive analysis of the training costs, hardware requirements, and environmental impact of frontier AI models, alongside an examination of the AI research community and open-source software ecosystem. 

Regarding training costs, the report highlights a significant upward trend. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman stated that training GPT-4 exceeded $100 million, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei noted in July 2024 that model training runs costing around $1 billion were already underway. In contrast, DeepSeek-V3 (2024) reportedly cost approximately $6 million to train, though some reports dispute this, arguing that actual development costs were higher when accounting for research expenses, capital expenditures, and employee salaries. To refine these estimates, the AI Index partnered with Epoch AI to analyze training duration, hardware type, quantity, and utilization rates using data from technical reports, press releases, and academic publications. 

Epoch AI's estimates, based on cloud compute rental prices, provide a comparative timeline of training costs: the original Transformer model (2017) cost approximately $670, RoBERTa Large (2019) cost approximately $160,000, OpenAI’s GPT-4 (2023) was estimated at $79 million, and Llama 3.1-405B (2024) had an estimated training cost of $170 million. The AI Index notes a direct correlation between a model's computational requirements and its training cost.

Hardware advancements have been critical in driving AI progress by reducing training time and accelerating complex computations. Machine learning hardware performance, measured in 16-bit floating-point operations, grew at an annual rate of approximately 43% between 2008 and 2024, doubling every 1.9 years. This progress is driven by specialized AI hardware, semiconductor manufacturing advancements, and increased transistor counts. Precision levels are optimized for different use cases: FP32 provides high precision for scientific computing, while lower-precision formats like FP16 and Tensor-FP16/BF16 are optimized for speed and energy efficiency, which is ideal for edge or mobile devices.

Specifically analyzing Nvidia data center GPUs, the H100 GPU (announced March 2022) achieves 22 billion FLOP per second per dollar, which is 1.7 times the price-performance of the A100 (June 2020) and 16.9 times that of the P100 (April 2016). Epoch AI estimates that the cost of hardware with a fixed performance level decreases by 30% annually. In terms of usage, the A100 was the most commonly reported hardware for training notable AI models, used by 64 models, followed by the V100; however, by the end of 2024, 15 models were reported as trained on the H100.

Energy efficiency, measured in FLOP/s per watt, has improved by approximately 40% per year. The Nvidia B100 (March 2024) achieved an energy efficiency of 2.5 trillion FLOP/s per watt, which is 33.8 times more energy efficient than the Nvidia P100 (April 2016), which reported 74 billion FLOP/s per watt. Despite these hardware efficiency gains, the total power consumption required to train frontier AI models is doubling annually due to the trend of training on larger datasets. For example, the original Transformer (2017) consumed an estimated 4,500 watts, PaLM consumed 2.6 million watts, and Llama 3.1-405B (summer 2024) required 25.3 million watts—over 5,000 times the power of the original Transformer.

This increase in power consumption has led to a corresponding rise in carbon emissions. Emissions from training AlexNet (2012) were negligible (0.01 tons of CO2 equivalent), while GPT-3 (2020) emitted around 588 tons of carbon, GPT-4 (2023) emitted 5,184 tons, and Llama 3.1 405B (2024) emitted 8,930 tons. DeepSeek V3 (2024), which has performance comparable to OpenAI’s o1, is estimated to have carbon emissions comparable to GPT-3 (2020). For comparison, the average American emits 18.08 tons of carbon per capita per year, a passenger flight from New York to San Francisco emits 0.99 tons, the average human life emits 5.51 tons per year, and average lifetime car usage (including fuel) emits 63 tons.

To estimate these emissions, the AI Index used developer-published carbon data and supplemented it with a widely used online AI training emissions calculator. This calculator estimates emissions based on training region, cloud provider, total training hours, and hardware type. The AI Index validated the calculator's accuracy by comparing its results with actual emissions reported by developers and found them to be largely consistent.

Beyond the environmental and financial costs of training, the report also analyzes the AI research community and professional networking. AI conferences have grown in scale and prestige over the last two decades. Total attendance at major AI conferences rose by more than 60,000 since 2014, with a 21.7% increase in attendance from 2023 to 2024. Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) remains the most attended conference, attracting nearly 20,000 participants in 2024. Other conferences with attendance increases in the last year include AAAI, ICLR, IROS, ICRA, ICML, and CVPR. A significant spike in ICML attendance in 2021 was attributed to the conference being held virtually. Total attendance figures include hybrid, virtual, and in-person participation.

Finally, the report examines open-source AI software via GitHub data. The number of AI-related GitHub projects has grown from 1,549 in 2011 to approximately 4.3 million in 2024, with a 40.3% increase in the last year alone. As of 2024, the United States contributes 23.4% of GitHub AI projects, followed by India (19.9%) and Europe (19.5%), though the U.S. share has declined since 2016. China accounts for 2.08% of the contributions. In 2024, the total number of new GitHub stars for AI-related projects rose from 14.0 million in 2023 to 17.7 million in 2024. In terms of cumulative GitHub stars, the United States leads with 21.08 million, followed by the 'Rest of the world' (16.39 million), Europe (10.29 million), India (4.06 million), and China (3.67 million). Popular libraries like PyTorch, Keras, TensorFlow, and OpenCV are among the most starred repositories.
block-L0-003.summary: The AI Index Report 2025 details the rise in AI training costs—with Llama 3.1-405B costing an estimated $170 million—and carbon emissions, which rose from 0.01 tons for AlexNet to 8,930 tons for Llama 3.1-405B. It also highlights the growth of the AI research community, including NeurIPS attracting nearly 20,000 participants in 2024, and AI-related GitHub projects growing to 4.3 million by 2024.

block-L0-004.context:
The Technical Performance chapter of the Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, provides an extensive analysis of AI technical progress in 2024. The report outlines a landscape characterized by the rapid mastery of new benchmarks, the convergence of frontier model performance, and a shrinking gap between open-weight and closed-weight models, as well as between US-based and Chinese models. 

### AI Performance Trends and Convergence
AI systems are mastering new benchmarks at an unprecedented pace. For tests introduced in 2023 to push the limits of AI, performance gains by 2024 were remarkable: MMMU saw an increase of 18.8 percentage points, and GPQA saw a 48.9 percentage point increase. On SWE-bench, AI ability to solve coding problems leaped from 4.4% in 2023 to 71.7% in 2024. In areas where humans still lead, the gap is closing; for instance, the state-of-the-art AI systems are now 7.9 percentage points ahead of human performance on the MATH benchmark for competition-level mathematics, compared to a 0.3-point gap in 2024. On the MMMU benchmark for multidisciplinary expert-level questions, the 2024 model o1 scored 78.2%, just 4.4 percentage points below the human benchmark of 82.6%.

There is a clear trend of performance convergence at the frontier. The Elo score difference between the top-ranked and 10th-ranked models on the LMSYS Chatbot Arena Leaderboard narrowed from 11.9% (as reported in the previous AI Index) to 5.4% by early 2025. Furthermore, the difference between the top two models shrank from 4.9% in 2023 to 0.7% in 2024. Current top providers include OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral AI, DeepSeek, and xAI.

### Open-Weight vs. Closed-Weight Models
The gap between closed-weight and open-weight models has narrowed significantly. In early January 2024, the leading closed-weight model outperformed the top open-weight model by 8.04% (or 8.0%) on the Chatbot Arena Leaderboard, but by February 2025, this gap shrank to 1.70% (or 1.7%). On the MMLU benchmark, closed-weight models led open models by 15.9 percentage points in late 2023, but this difference fell to 0.1 percentage point by the end of 2024. This shift was largely driven by the release of Meta's Llama 3.1 and DeepSeek's V3.

Models are categorized by their level of openness. Entirely closed models include Google's Med-Gemini. Limited access models, provided via API but without released weights, include OpenAI's GPT-4o and Anthropic's Claude 3.5. Open-weight models, where weights are available for modification, include Meta's Llama 3.3 and Stable Video 4D. While open-weight models are more accessible, they are not strictly 'open source' because training data and underlying code are often withheld. Advocates argue they prevent monopolies and spur innovation—citing the use of Llama in military applications and the creation of Meditron—while critics warn of security risks, such as the creation of bioweapons or disinformation.

### Global Competition: US vs. China
The technical performance gap between the US and China is closing. In January 2024, the top US model outperformed the best Chinese model by 9.3% on the LMSYS Chatbot Arena, but by February 2025, the gap was 1.7%. At the end of 2023, the performance gaps on MMLU, MMMU, MATH, and HumanEval were 17.5, 13.5, 24.3, and 31.6 percentage points, respectively. By the end of 2024, these gaps narrowed to 0.3, 8.1, 1.6, and 3.7 percentage points. The launch of DeepSeek-R1 was particularly notable as it achieved these results using only a fraction of the hardware resources typically required, casting doubt on the effectiveness of US semiconductor export controls.

### Model Efficiency and Compact Models
While scaling has driven progress, 2024 saw a breakthrough in smaller, high-performing models, including Llama 3.1 8B, o1-mini, GPT-4o mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash, and Mistral Small 3.5. These compact models offer higher algorithmic efficiency, lower training costs, and faster inference. This is exemplified by the MMLU benchmark: in 2022, the smallest model to score over 60% was PaLM (540 billion parameters); by 2024, Microsoft's Phi-3-mini achieved this with only 3.8 billion parameters, a 142-fold reduction in size.

### Reasoning Paradigms and Agentic AI
New reasoning paradigms, specifically test-time compute and iterative reasoning, have improved performance. OpenAI's o1 and o3 models use these techniques. The o1 model scored 74.4% on an International Mathematical Olympiad qualifying exam, whereas GPT-4o scored 9.3%. However, o1 is nearly six times more expensive and 30 times slower than GPT-4o. 

AI agents are showing early promise. The 2024 launch of RE-Bench provides a rigorous benchmark for agents. In short time-horizon settings (two-hour budget), top AI systems score four times higher than human experts. However, in 32-hour budget settings, humans still outscore AI two to one. AI agents already match human expertise in specific tasks like writing Triton kernels, operating at lower costs and higher speeds.

### Benchmarking Challenges and the Turing Test
Benchmarks are essential but flawed. The BetterBench study analyzed 24 benchmarks and found 14 failed to report statistical significance, 17 lacked replication scripts, and most had poor documentation. In Figure 2.1.41 of the report, MMLU showed poor adherence to quality standards, while GPQA performed better. Contamination—where models are trained on test questions—is a common issue, specifically noted in many LLMs' performance on the GSM8K mathematics benchmark. To combat this, LiveBench was introduced to provide periodically updated questions from unfamiliar sources.

Additionally, the Turing test, proposed by Alan Turing in 1950, is becoming less relevant as modern LLMs have advanced to the point where humans struggle to differentiate them from machines in text-based conversations. In robotics, new benchmarks like ARMBench focus on perception, while VIMA-Bench assesses simulated environments incorporating perception, communication, and deep learning.

### Natural Language Processing and MMLU
In NLP, state-of-the-art models like Gemini, Claude 3.5, and GPT-4o can reason across audio, images, and goal-oriented tasks. The Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) benchmark, created in 2020, tests performance across 57 subjects. OpenAI’s o1-preview achieved the highest recorded MMLU score of 92.3% in September 2024, compared to 86.4% for GPT-4 (March 2023) and 27.9% for RoBERTa in 2019—a 64.4 percentage point increase over five years. The human baseline is 89.8%. 

Due to MMLU's simplistic questions, MMLU-Pro was introduced in 2024 to remove trivialities and increase answer choices; DeepSeek-R1 currently holds the highest score on MMLU-Pro at 84.0%. To evaluate public preference, the LMSYS Chatbot Arena Leaderboard uses anonymous voting. As of early 2025, it has over 1 million votes, with a Google Gemini model as the most preferred. 

To reduce human curation costs, UC Berkeley researchers created BenchBuilder, an automated pipeline using LLMs to curate prompts. This was used to develop Arena-Hard-Auto, which uses 500 challenging queries with GPT-4 Turbo as the judge against a baseline (GPT-4-0314). As of November 2024, the top scores on Arena-Hard-Auto were o1-mini (92.0), o1-preview (90.4), and Claude-3.5-Sonnet (85.2). However, the November variant of Claude 3.5 Sonnet leads the style leaderboard.

### Significant Model and Dataset Releases of 2024
Throughout 2024, a high volume of notable AI releases occurred:
- **January 19:** Stable LM 2 (Stability AI) - 1.6B parameters, for portable devices.
- **February 8:** Aya Dataset (Cohere for AI, Beijing Academy of AI, Cohere, Binghamton University) - 513 million prompt-completion pairs in 114 languages.
- **February 15:** Gemini 1.5 Pro (Google DeepMind) - 1 million token context window, exceeding GPT-4 Turbo's 128K.
- **February 20:** SDXL-Lightning (ByteDance) - Fast text-to-image using progressive adversarial distillation.
- **February 25:** Claude 3 (Anthropic) - Outperforms GPT-4 and Gemini on benchmarks while reducing prompt refusals.
- **March 4:** Claude 3 (Anthropic) - (Note: Child context lists March 4 for Claude 3).
- **March 7:** Inflection-2.5 (Inflection AI) - GPT-4 level performance using 40% of GPT-4's compute; Microsoft acquired Inflection for $650 million two weeks later.
- **March 19:** Moirai and LOTSA (Salesforce) - Moirai is a foundation model for forecasting; LOTSA is a time series dataset with 27 billion observations in nine domains.
- **March 27:** DBRX (Databricks) - Open-source MoE transformer decoder-only model (132B parameters, 36B active), trained on 12 trillion tokens.
- **April 2:** Stable Audio 2 (Stability AI) - Song generator with audio-to-audio functionality.
- **April 17:** Llama 3 (Meta) - 8B and 70B parameter models.
- **May 13:** GPT-4o (OpenAI) - Multimodal model (text, audio, images, video) with audio responses in as little as 320 milliseconds.
- **June 7:** Qwen2 (Alibaba) - Base and instruction-tuned models rivaling Llama 3-70B and Mixtral-8x22B.
- **June 17:** Runway Gen-3 (Runway) - Text-to-video/image-to-video focusing on photorealistic humans.
- **July 23:** Llama 3.1 405B (Meta) - Most capable open-weight foundation model, rivaling closed models.
- **August 12:** Falcon Mamba (TII Abu Dhabi) - 7B parameter model using Mamba State Space Language Model (SSLM) architecture.
- **August 13:** Grok-2 (xAI) - Advanced reasoning and problem-solving model.
- **August 15:** Imagen 3 (Google Labs) - Highest Elo score on GenAI-Bench image benchmark.
- **August 22:** Jamba 1.5 (AI21 Labs) - Combines state-space models with transformers.
- **August 29:** SynthID v2 (Google) - Watermarking tool for AI-generated content.
- **September 11:** NotebookLM Podcast Tool (Google Labs) - End-to-end AI podcast generator.
- **September 12:** o1-preview (OpenAI) - First of 'o series' for advanced reasoning in math, science, and coding.
- **September 19:** Qwen2.5 (Alibaba) - Foundation models including specialized coding and math models.
- **September 17:** NVLM (D, H, X) (Nvidia) - Open-access vision-language models achieving top scores on VQAv2 and OCRBench.
- **October 16:** Ministral (Mistral) - 3B and 8B parameter models outperforming Gemma and Llama of similar size.
- **October 22:** Anthropic Computer Use (Anthropic) - Claude 3.5 Sonnet feature for autonomous cursor/typing in real time.
- **October 28:** Apple Intelligence (Apple) - Suite including Image Playground, Genmoji, and Siri integration with ChatGPT.
- **December 3:** Nova Pro (Amazon) - AWS Nova family, specializes in financial documents.
- **December 11:** Gemini 2 (Google DeepMind) - Twice as fast as Gemini 1.5 Pro, includes computer control and image/audio generation.
- **December 12:** Sora (OpenAI) - Video generation (1080p up to 20s for Pro, 720p up to 5s for ChatGPT Plus).
- **December 13:** Global MMLU (Cohere) - Multilingual MMLU translation in 42 languages.
- **December 20:** o3 (beta) (OpenAI) - Frontier model for PhD-level science, research math, and SWE, achieving 87.5% on ARC-AGI private holdout set.
- **December 27:** DeepSeek-V3 (DeepSeek) - Open-source model outperforming leading models on GPQA and MMLU.

### Final Technical Considerations
Despite these advances, complex reasoning remains a persistent problem. LLMs still struggle with logical reasoning, arithmetic, and planning, especially on instances larger than those they were trained on, limiting their reliability in high-risk applications. High-quality AI video generators, such as SORA, Veo 2, Google DeepMind, Movie Gen (Meta), and Stable Video 3D and 4D, showed significant improvement in 2024 over 2023 versions. 

Additionally, a new class of benchmarks like Humanity’s Last Exam (top score 8.80%), FrontierMath (solve only 2% of problems), and BigCodeBench (35.5% success rate vs. human 97%) have been introduced to replace saturated traditional benchmarks like MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval.
block-L0-004.summary: The Technical Performance chapter of the AI Index Report 2025 details how AI models in 2024 achieved unprecedented benchmark gains (e.g., SWE-bench rising from 4.4% to 71.7%) and closed the gap between open-weight and closed-weight models, as well as US and Chinese models (e.g., MMLU gap narrowing from 17.5 to 0.3 percentage points). It also highlights the lauch of advanced models like OpenAI's o1 and o3, and the lauch of Meta's Llama 3.1 405B.

block-L0-005.context:
The Technical Performance chapter of the Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, provides an extensive analysis of AI benchmarks and model capabilities across language, vision, video, speech, and coding. 

### Language and Reasoning

In the domain of language, several new benchmarks and reasoning paradigms have emerged. The Arena-Hard-Auto benchmark, which leverages an automated pipeline called BenchBuilder to curate 500 challenging queries from the Chatbot Arena, uses GPT-4 Turbo as a judge against a baseline model (GPT-4-0314). More than 50% of its questions focus on coding and debugging. As of November 2024, the top scores on Arena-Hard-Auto were o1-mini (92.0), o1-preview (90.4), and Claude-3.5-Sonnet (85.2). Additionally, the benchmark features a style control leaderboard to assess how response style influences preference; the November variant of Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 3.5 is the top model on this specific leaderboard.

WildBench, developed in 2024 by researchers from the Allen Institute for AI and the University of Washington, addresses the limitations of academic-focused benchmarks like MMLU and human-heavy benchmarks like LMSYS by using diverse "in the wild" questions from over 1 million human-chatbot interactions. Currently, GPT-4o is the top-performing model on WildBench with an Elo score of 1227.1, followed by Claude 3.5 Sonnet with a score of 1215.4.

MixEval, launched by researchers from the National University of Singapore, Carnegie Mellon University, and the Allen Institute for AI, combines real-world user queries with ground-truth-based questions. On the MixEval-Hard suite, OpenAI’s o1-preview achieved the highest score of 72.0, followed by Claude 3.5 Sonnet-0620 (68.1) and Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct (66.2), all released in 2024.

OpenAI's o1 and o3 models represent a shift toward advanced reasoning through inference or test-time computation, utilizing a chain-of-thought process to break complex problems into smaller steps and iteratively check answers. This approach allows o1 to provide more thorough reasoning than GPT-4 when deciphering scrambled text. In head-to-head comparisons, o1 outperforms GPT-4o by 2.8 points on MMLU, 34.5 points on MATH, 26.7 points on GPQA Diamond, and 65.1 points on AIME 2024 (where o1 scored 74.4% vs GPT-4o's 9.3%). Furthermore, the o3 model achieved an 87.5% accuracy rate on the ARC-AGI benchmark, surpassing the previous record of 55.5%. 

However, these reasoning capabilities come with higher costs and latency. GPT-4o costs $2.50 per 1 million input tokens and $10 per 1 million output tokens, while o1 costs $15 per 1 million input tokens and $60 per 1 million output tokens. Additionally, o1 is approximately 40 times slower than GPT-4o, with a time to first token of 29.7 seconds compared to 0.72 seconds for GPT-4o. OpenAI released o1-preview to ChatGPT Plus and Teams users on September 12, 2024, and the full version of o1 and the $200 monthly ChatGPT Pro subscription on December 5, 2024. The o3 model remains restricted to select researchers and developers via a safety testing program.

### RAG, Embeddings, and Long-Context Retrieval

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) capabilities have evolved, with Anthropic introducing Contextual Retrieval in September 2024 to enhance these processes. New benchmarks for RAG include Ragnarok, CRAG, and FinanceBench for financial question answering. 

The Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB), created by Hugging Face and Cohere in late 2022, evaluates how models convert data into numerical embedding vectors across 58 datasets, 112 languages, and eight tasks: bitext mining, classification, clustering, pair classification, reranking, retrieval, semantic textual similarity, and summarization. As of early 2025, the top-performing embedding model is Voyage AI’s voyage-3-m-exp (score of 74.03), which uses quantization-aware training and Matryoshka Representation Learning. This model narrowly beat NV-Embed-v2, which held the top spot for most of 2024 with a score of 72.31. The leading model's score has risen from 59.5 in late 2022 to the current high.

Regarding long-context retrieval, models have shifted from simple "needle-in-the-haystack" tests to more complex evaluations. Context windows have expanded from 2023 models like GPT-4 and Llama 2 (8,000 and 4,000 tokens, respectively) to modern models like GPT-4o (May 2024) and Gemini 2.0 Pro Experimental (February 2025), which range from 128 thousand to 2 million tokens. 

To evaluate these expanded windows, Nvidia’s RULER benchmark assesses multihop reasoning, aggregation, and retrieval performance. Gemini-1.5-Pro achieved the highest weighted performance average of 95.5 on RULER, followed by GPT-4 (89.0) and GLM4 (88.0). RULER also found that only half of the popular LLMs claiming context sizes of 32K tokens or greater can actually maintain satisfactory performance at that length. Similarly, HELMET (How to Evaluate Long-Context Models Effectively and Thoroughly), a collaboration between Intel and Princeton, uses seven categories including passage re-ranking and synthetic recall. On HELMET (across 8K, 32K, and 128K settings), Gemini 1.5 Pro and the August variant of GPT-4 maintained effectiveness, while GPT-4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Llama 3.1-70B showed performance degradation.

### Computer Vision and Image/Video Generation

In computer vision, benchmarks have moved from simple classification (ImageNet) to complex reasoning. The Visual Commonsense Reasoning (VCR) challenge (2019) tests the ability to provide rationales for answers. In July 2024, a model reached a Q->AR score of 85.0, matching the human benchmark and improving 4.2% over 2023. For video understanding, the MVBench benchmark (2023) requires temporal reasoning. As of 2024, the top model is Video-CCAM-7B-v1.2 (based on Qwen 2.5-7B-Instruct) with a score of 69.23, a 14.6% improvement since late 2023.

Image generation has progressed to the point where human faces are frequently indistinguishable from real photos. Midjourney's evolution from 2022 to 2025 shows a shift from cartoonish renderings to startlingly realistic depictions. Public preference is measured via the Chatbot Arena's Vision Arena, which has over 150,000 votes on prompts like "Batman drinking a coffee." As of early 2025, the top-ranked model is Google’s Gemini-2.0-Flash-Thinking-Exp-1219, with only a 3.4% gap between it and the fourth-ranked ChatGPT-4o-latest (2024-1120).

Video generation saw a significant leap in 2024. Stability AI launched Stable Video Diffusion (November 2023) and Stable Video 3D (March 2024), the latter generating 3D views from a single image. OpenAI previewed Sora in February 2024 and released it in December 2024, capable of 1080p 20-second videos. Meta unveiled Movie Gen in October 2024, which creates 16-second 1080p videos at 16 fps, incorporating sound and personalized video generation. Google launched Veo (May 2024) and Veo 2 (December 2024); internal benchmarks showed Veo 2 outperforming Movie Gen, Kling v1.5, and Sora Turbo. Other notable generators include Runway’s Gen-3 Alpha, Luma’s Dream Machine, and Kuaishou’s Kling 1.5. Improvement is evidenced by the "Will Smith eating spaghetti" prompt, where Pika's 2025 versions are vastly superior to 2023 versions.

### Speech and Coding

Speech recognition is evaluated on the LRS2 (Oxford-BBC Lip Reading Sentences 2) benchmark (2017), using Word Error Rate (WER). The model Whisper-Flamingo achieved a new standard with a WER of 1.3%, though the report suggests this benchmark may be nearing saturation.

Coding capabilities are evaluated through complex challenges as foundational benchmarks like HumanEval (164 problems) are now saturated—Claude 3.5 Sonnet (HPT) achieved a score of 100%. SWE-bench (October 2023), using 2,294 GitHub problems, shows a dramatic rise in performance: while the best model at the end of 2023 scored 4.4%, OpenAI’s o3 solved 71.7% by early 2025. On BigCodeBench (2024), which tests functions across 139 libraries, the best model, OpenAI’s o1, scored 35.5 on the hard subset. On the Chatbot Arena LLM leaderboard's coding filter, Gemini-Exp-1206 leads with a score of 1,369, followed by o1 at 1,361.
block-L0-005.summary: The AI Index Report 2025 highlights significant leaps in AI reasoning (OpenAI o1/o3), long-context retrieval (Gemini 1.5 Pro), and coding (o3 solving 71.7% of SWE-bench), while noting the saturation of early benchmarks like HumanEval.

block-L0-006.context:
The Technical Performance chapter of the Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, provides a comprehensive analysis of AI model performance across coding, mathematics, reasoning, and agentic capabilities. 

### AI Performance in Coding and Mathematics

In the domain of coding, the LMSYS Chatbot Arena for LLMs coding filter indicates that among Chinese models, DeepSeek-V3 leads with an Elo score of 1,317, trailing the highest-ranking model by 3.8%.

Mathematical problem-solving is evaluated using benchmarks that span from grade-school to competition-level mathematics. The GSM8K benchmark, introduced by OpenAI in 2021, contains approximately 8,000 diverse grade-school math word problems requiring multistep arithmetic solutions. The top-performing model on GSM8K is a variant of Claude Sonnet 3.5 optimized using the HPT prompting strategy, which achieved a score of 97.72%, a significant increase from the 2023 high of 91.00%. However, in 2024, several models from Mistral, Meta, and Qwen scored around 96%, suggesting that the GSM8K benchmark may be approaching saturation.

For more challenging tasks, the MATH dataset, introduced in 2021 by UC Berkeley and University of Chicago researchers, contains 12,500 competition-level mathematics problems. While AI systems initially solved only 6.9% of these problems, OpenAI’s o3-mini (high) model achieved a record score of 97.9% in January 2025, surpassing the human baseline of 90%.

Public preference in mathematics is tracked via the Chatbot Arena's math filter, which has collected over 340,000 public votes across 181 models. While Gemini-based models lead in the general and coding arenas, the top-ranked model in the Math Arena is an OpenAI o1 variant released in December 2024.

To address the saturation of high school and college-level benchmarks, Epoch AI introduced FrontierMath. This benchmark features hundreds of original, exceptionally challenging problems in areas such as number theory, real analysis, algebraic geometry, and category theory. Upon initial release, Gemini 1.5 Pro was the best-performing model but solved only 2.0% of the problems; other leading models, including o1-preview, o1-mini, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Grok 2 Beta, also showed very low success rates. However, OpenAI’s o3 model is reported to have scored 25.2% on FrontierMath.

In the area of theorem proving, Google DeepMind developed AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry 2 for the 2024 International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO). AlphaProof, a reinforcement learning system derived from AlphaZero, uses a fine-tuned Gemini model to translate natural language problems into the Lean formal proof system. AlphaGeometry 2 is a neuro-symbolic hybrid system using a Gemini-based language model trained on synthetic data. Together, they solved four out of six problems in the 2024 IMO: AlphaProof solved two algebra problems and one number theory problem, while AlphaGeometry 2 solved the sole geometry problem in 24 seconds. This performance level is equivalent to an IMO silver medalist, who typically solves 22.9 geometry problems in the IMO-AG-30 benchmarking set, whereas AlphaGeometry solved 25 out of 30 problems.

### AI Reasoning and General Intelligence

As older benchmarks like SQuAD and VQA have become saturated, researchers from the United States and Canada developed the Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark (MMMU). MMMU consists of approximately 11,500 college-level questions across six core disciplines: art and design, business, science, health and medicine, humanities and social science, and technology and engineering. As of January 2025, OpenAI’s o1 is the highest-performing model on MMMU with a score of 78.2%, improving upon the state-of-the-art score of 59.4% reported in the 2024 AI Index, though it remains below the human expert baseline of 82.6%.

Regarding general, multisubject AI reasoning, researchers from NYU, Anthropic, and Meta introduced the GPQA benchmark to test AI systems. The GPQA dataset contains 448 difficult multiple-choice questions crafted by subject-matter experts in biology, physics, and chemistry, designed to be resistant to simple web searches. In the 2023 AI Index, the best-performing model, GPT-4, achieved a score of 38.8% on the GPQA diamond test set (the most challenging subset). By December 2024, OpenAI's o3 model achieved a state-of-the-art score of 87.7% on the diamond set, representing a 48.9 percentage point improvement over the 2023 state-of-the-art and becoming the first model to exceed the baseline accuracy of 81.3% set by expert human validators.

To evaluate the ability of AI systems to generalize beyond prior training, François Chollet (creator of the Keras deep learning library) introduced the ARC-AGI benchmark in 2019. ARC-AGI presents AI systems with independent tasks featuring demonstration or input pairs followed by test or output scenarios, requiring assumed prior knowledge (such as basic topology, objects, and elementary arithmetic) rather than specialized world knowledge. In 2020, the top-performing system on ARC-AGI scored 20%, and by 2024, the score rose to 33%. However, OpenAI's o3 model achieved a score of 75.7%, and when allocated a high compute budget exceeding the benchmark's $10,000 limit, it reached a score of 87.5%. Researchers suggest that previous slow progress was due to an overemphasis on scaling model size and training data, whereas recent gains indicate a shift toward improving search capabilities and generalization.

Due to the saturation of benchmarks like MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval, the team behind MMLU introduced Humanity's Last Exam (HLE), a benchmark comprising 2,700 highly challenging multimodal questions across dozens of subject areas. These questions were contributed by leading professors and graduate-level reviewers and were specifically tested against state-of-the-art LLMs before inclusion to ensure no existing model could answer them. Initial testing shows HLE is extremely difficult; OpenAI's o1 scores only 8.8%, while Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking (7.2%), Gemini 1.5 Pro (5.2%), Claude 3.5 Sonnet (4.8%), Grok-2 (3.9%), and GPT-4o (3.1%) score even lower. Researchers speculate that performance could exceed 50% by the end of 2025.

### Planning and Agentic Capabilities

In the domain of planning—reasoning about actions that alter the world—Arizona State University proposed PlanBench, a suite of 600 problems based on the International Planning Competition. PlanBench tests models on tasks such as constructing stacks of blocks (Blocksworld), where a hand can only move one block at a time. In the Blocksworld zero-shot evaluation, OpenAI's o1 scored 97.8%, significantly outperforming Llama 3.1 405B (62.6%) and GPT-4o (35.5%). In the more difficult Mystery Blocksworld domain, where answers are syntactically obfuscated, o1 scored 52.8%, while Llama 3.1 405B scored 0.8% and GPT-4 scored 0%. Despite these gains, o1 solves only 23.6% of planning instances that require at least 20 steps.

Additionally, the report discusses AI agents—autonomous or semiautonomous systems designed to accomplish goals in specific environments. Because agentic tasks are diverse and dynamic, they are harder to benchmark than image classification. In 2024, VisualAgentBench (VAB) was launched to test agents in three categories: embodied agents (household and gaming), GUI agents (mobile and web apps), and GraphQL design agents (CSS debugging). On the VAB test set, GPT-4o achieved the highest overall success rate at 36.2%, while most proprietary models averaged around 20%.

To test the R&D capabilities of AI systems, researchers launched RE-Bench in 2024, featuring seven open-ended machine learning research environments, such as optimizing a kernel or fine-tuning GPT-2. In short time-horizon settings (two-hour budget), the best AI systems score four times higher than human experts. In a 32-hour budget setting, however, humans outperform AI by a factor of two. In certain tasks, such as writing custom Triton kernels, AI agents can complete the work more quickly than any human expert.
block-L0-006.summary: The AI Index Report 2025 analyzes technical performance across coding, math, and reasoning, highlighting records such as OpenAI's o3 achieving 97.9% on the MATH dataset and 87.7% on the GPQA diamond set, while noting the saturation of benchmarks like GSM8K.

block-L0-007.context:
The Technical Performance chapter of the Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, provides a comprehensive analysis of advancements in AI reasoning, general-purpose assistants, robotics, and autonomous motion. 

Regarding general AI assistants, Meta introduced the GAIA benchmark in May 2024 to assess the ability of AI systems to perform a broad range of tasks, including reasoning, multimodal processing, web browsing, and tool use. GAIA consists of 466 questions that challenge models with complex, multistep problems requiring open web searches, the interpretation of multimodal inputs, and reasoning through intricate scenarios. When GAIA was first launched, Large Language Models (LLMs) significantly lagged behind human performance; for instance, GPT-4 with plugins correctly answered only 15% of the questions, while human respondents scored 92%. By 2024, the top system on GAIA reached a score of 65.1%, representing a roughly 30 percentage point increase over the highest score recorded in 2023.

In the field of robotics, the Robot Learning Benchmark (RLBench), launched in 2019, is one of the most widely adopted benchmarks and features 100 unique tasks ranging from simple target reaching to opening an oven and placing a tray inside. Evaluation typically focuses on a standardized subset of 18 tasks. As of January 2025, the top-performing model on this subset is SAM2Act—a collaboration between the University of Washington, Universidad Católica San Pablo, Nvidia, and the Allen Institute for AI—which achieved an 86.8% success rate. This is a 2.8 percentage point improvement over the 2024 state-of-the-art and a 66.7 percentage point increase from the leading score in 2021.

Humanoid robotics saw significant growth in 2024. Figure AI launched Figure 02, a general-purpose humanoid robot standing 5 feet 6 inches tall, weighing 154 pounds, and capable of handling a 44-pound payload. Figure 02 can operate for up to five hours on a single charge and can perform tasks such as making coffee and assisting in automotive assembly by placing sheet metal into a car fixture. Integrated with OpenAI, Figure 02 can engage in speech-to-speech reasoning to explain its actions and respond to queries. Other notable humanoid robots include Tesla’s Optimus (first launched in 2002 and redesigned in 2023) and Boston Dynamics’ Atlas.

Google DeepMind has also made significant strides in robotic advancements. In 2023, DeepMind launched PaLM-E and RT-2, which utilized transformer-based architectures and training on both manipulation and language data to excel at both robotic manipulation and text generation. In 2024, DeepMind introduced AutoRT, an AI system that uses foundation models to autonomously generate training data by coordinating multiple video-equipped robots, resulting in a dataset of 77,000 robotic trials across 6,650 unique tasks. DeepMind also developed SARA-RT, which uses "up-training" to convert the quadratic complexity of standard transformers into a linear model, reducing computational demands while maintaining performance. Other DeepMind contributions include the ALOHA (Autonomous and DemoStart Learning of High-level Activities) approach, allowing robots to perform intricate tasks such as tying shoelaces, hanging a shirt, and stacking kitchen items, and DemoStart, an auto-curriculum reinforcement learning method for mastering complex behaviors using sparse rewards and limited demonstrations. Furthermore, DeepMind introduced a robotic model in 2024 capable of reaching amateur human-level performance in competitive table tennis.

There was a significant push toward robotic foundation models in 2024. Nvidia introduced GR00T (Generalist Robot 00 Technology), a general-purpose foundation model for humanoid robots designed to mimic human movements and understand natural language, accompanied by data pipelines, simulation frameworks, and the Thor robotics computer. Other robotic foundation models include Covariant's RFM-1, which features language reasoning and real-world maneuverability, and LLaRA, developed by researchers at Stony Brook University and the University of Wisconsin-Madison, which integrates perception, communication, and action into a single deep learning model. These models build upon the 2023 trend of RT-2, PaLM-E, and Open-X Embodiment.

Regarding self-driving cars, Waymo (a subsidiary of Alphabet) operates robotaxis in Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Austin. As of January 2025, Waymo provides 150,000 paid rides per week, covering over a million miles. Through September 2024, Waymo recorded the following rider-only miles: 20.823 million in Phoenix, 10.209 million in San Francisco, 1.947 million in Los Angeles, and 124,000 in Austin. Waymo also plans to test vehicles in 10 additional cities, including Las Vegas, San Diego, and Miami, and has tested in snowy conditions in upstate New York and Truckee, California. 

In China, Baidu’s Apollo Go reported 988,000 rides in Q3 2024, a 20% year-over-year increase. As of October 2024, Apollo Go operated 400 robotaxis with plans to expand to 1,000 by the end of 2025. Pony.AI also plans to scale its fleet from 200 to between 2,000 and 3,000 vehicles by the end of 2026. China is currently testing more driverless cars than any other country and is rolling them out across 16 cities. In Europe, startups like Wayve are also gaining traction.

Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in October 2024, a two-passenger autonomous vehicle without a steering wheel or pedals, expected to enter production in 2026 at a price under $30,000. Tesla also unveiled the Robovan, an electric autonomous van capable of transporting up to 20 passengers. In China, Baidu's Apollo Go launched the RT6 robotaxi, which features a battery-swapping system and a price the price tag of $30,000. Additionally, Uber has partnered with WeRide—the first publicly listed robotaxi company—to develop an autonomous ride-sharing platform in Abu Dhabi.

In the realm of autonomous freight, companies like Kodiak have completed their first driverless deliveries. Aurora has reported over 1 million miles of autonomous freight hauling on U.S. highways since 2021, though these miles were completed with human safety drivers present. Aurora has delayed the commercial launch of its fleet from the end of 2024 to April 2025.

To evaluate these capabilities, new benchmarks were introduced in 2024. NuPlan, developed by Motional, is a large-scale autonomous driving dataset and evaluation framework for testing machine-learning-based motion planners, featuring 1,282 hours of diverse driving scenarios and a training set of over 2 million fully annotated frames from more than 10,000 clips. Bench2Drive provides a comprehensive, realistic, closed-loop testing simulation environment for end-to-end autonomous vehicles to address the limitations of open-loop evaluations. According to Bench2Drive, top performers include TCP* (64.22), DriveAdapter (49.30), and ThinkTwice (40.73). OpenAD is the first real-world, open-world autonomous driving benchmark for 3D object detection, focusing on domain generalization and open-vocabulary recognition.

Safety data suggests that self-driving cars may be safer than human drivers. Waymo data for Phoenix and San Francisco shows significantly fewer incidents per million miles than human benchmarks: 0.32 airbag deployments compared to 5.91 for humans, 0.90 injury-reported crashes compared to 40.06 for humans, and 1.74 police-reported incidents compared to 2.26 for humans. Specifically, the percentage difference to the human benchmark is -88% for airbag deployments in Phoenix and -87% in San Francisco, -78% for injury-reported crashes in Phoenix and -78% in San Francisco, and -77% for police-reported incidents in Phoenix and -88% in San Francisco. 

Furthermore, a study by Waymo and Swiss Re analyzed liability claims across 25.3 million miles driven. The study found that Waymo vehicles had an 88% reduction in property damage claims and a 92% reduction in bodily injury claims compared to human-driver baselines. In real terms, Waymo vehicles were involved in only nine property damage claims and two bodily injury claims over that distance, whereas human drivers would be expected to incur 78 property damage claims and 26 bodily injury claims.
