chunk-007.context:
The Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, includes a section on global AI patents and notable AI models. 

Regarding AI patents, the report utilizes patent-level bibliographic records from PATSTAT Global, a comprehensive database provided by the European Patent Office (EPO). Due to data availability delays, 2023 is the most recent year with accessible data. From 2010 to 2023, the number of granted AI patents worldwide grew steadily from 3,833 to 122,511, with a 29.6% increase in the last year (2023).

In terms of regional distribution, 82.4% of the world's granted AI patents as of 2023 originated from East Asia and the Pacific, followed by North America at 14.2%. The gap in AI patent grants between East Asia and the Pacific and North America has widened steadily since 2010. Disaggregated by geographic area, China led with 69.7% of granted AI patents in 2023, followed by the United States at 14.2%. The share of AI patents from the United States declined from a peak of 42.8% in 2015. 

When analyzing AI patents per 100,000 inhabitants in 2023, South Korea had the most with 17.27, followed by Luxembourg (15.31), China (6.08), the United States (5.20), and Japan (4.58). Between 2013 and 2023, Luxembourg (8,216%), China (6,317%), and Sweden (3,453%) experienced the greatest percentage increase in AI patenting per capita.

Additionally, the report examines "notable machine learning models," a term defined by the data provider Epoch AI to designate influential models selected based on state-of-the-art advancements, historical significance, or high citation rates. In 2024, the United States led in the production of notable AI models with 40 models, followed by China with 15 and France with three. All major geographic groups, including the United States, China, and Europe, released fewer notable models in 2024 than in 2023. Since 2003, the United States has produced more notable models than other major countries such as the United Kingdom, China, and Canada.

By sector, industry has led in releasing notable machine learning models since 2014. In 2024, industry produced 55 notable AI models, and Epoch AI identified no notable AI models originating from academia in 2024. The proportion of notable AI models originating from industry grew to 90.2% in 2024. By organization, Google led the production of notable models over the past decade with 187 models, followed by Meta (82) and Microsoft (39). In 2024, the top contributors were Google (7 models), OpenAI (7 models), and Alibaba (6 models). Among academic institutions since 2014, Carnegie Mellon University (25), Stanford University (25), and Tsinghua University (22) have been the most prolific.

chunk-008.context:
The Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, provides detailed data on notable AI models from 2014 to 2024. According to data from Epoch AI, the organizations that produced the most notable AI models in this period were Google (187 models), Meta (82), Microsoft (39), OpenAI (36), Carnegie Mellon University (25), Stanford University (25), Tsinghua University (22), UC Berkeley (22), Nvidia (17), the University of Oxford (16), MIT (15), Salesforce (15), the University of Washington (15), Alibaba (14), and the Allen Institute for AI (12). Research published by DeepMind is classified under Google in these figures. 

Notable AI models are released under various access types. API access allows users to interact with models via queries without direct access to weights; Hosted access (no API) refers to models available through a platform interface without programmatic access (e.g., Gemini 2.0 Pro); Open weights (restricted use) provide weights but impose limitations, such as prohibiting commercial use or redistribution (e.g., DeepSeek-V3); Open weights (unrestricted) are fully open, allowing free use, modification, and redistribution (e.g., AlphaGeometry); Open weights (noncommercial) share weights but restrict use to research or noncommercial purposes (e.g., Mistral Large 2); and unreleased models remain private (e.g., ESM3 98B). The designation 'unknown' is used for models with unclear access types. In 2024, API access was the most common release type, with 20 of 61 models made available this way. Over time, API access has seen a steady rise since 2020; in 2024, 32.8% of notable AI models were released via API access, followed by Open weights (restricted use) at 18.03%, Unreleased at 16.39%, Open weights (unrestricted) at 11.48%, Open weights (noncommercial) at 9.84%, and Hosted access (no API) at 8.20%, with 3.28% classified as Unknown.

Regarding training code, 60.7% of notable AI models launched in 2024 were released without corresponding training code, contrasting with traditional open-source software where all components are typically made available.

Model parameters—numerical values learned during training—have risen sharply since the early 2010s. High-parameter models typically outperform those with fewer parameters but require more data and financial resources for training, a trend particularly evident in the industry sector. The training dataset sizes for Large Language Models (LLMs) double approximately every eight months. For example, the Transformer model (2017) was trained on approximately 2 billion tokens, GPT-3 175B (davinci) was trained on an estimated 374 billion tokens, and Meta’s Llama 3.3 (2024) was trained on roughly 15 trillion tokens.

Training times have also increased. AlexNet (2012) trained in five to six days on less advanced hardware, whereas Llama 3.1-405B required approximately 90 days to train, and Google’s Gemini 1.0 Ultra (2023) took around 100 days.

Compute refers to the computational resources required to train and operate a model. Training compute for notable AI models doubles roughly every five months, a trend especially pronounced in the last five years. For instance, AlexNet (2012) required an estimated 470 petaFLOP, the original Transformer (2017) required around 7,400 petaFLOP, and GPT-4o required 38 billion petaFLOP.
chunk-008.summary: Between 2014 and 2024, Google led in notable AI model production with 187 models, while in 2024, API access became the most common release type at 32.8%. Training compute for these models has doubled every five months, with GPT-4o requiring 38 billion petaFLOP compared to AlexNet's 470 petaFLOP.

chunk-009.context:
The Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, provides detailed analysis on the development and costs of notable AI models. 

Regarding training compute, the launch of DeepSeek’s V3 model in December 2024 gained significant attention because it achieved high performance while requiring fewer computational resources than many leading Large Language Models (LLMs). According to Epoch AI, top 10 Chinese language models have scaled their training compute at a rate of approximately three times per year since late 2021, which is considerably slower than the five times per year trend observed in the rest of the world since 2018. Top-tier AI models from the United States have generally been more computationally intensive than those from China.

There is an ongoing debate regarding whether AI models will run out of training data. One key driver of algorithmic improvements has been the scaling of models on ever-larger datasets, but concerns have grown about a potential data bottleneck as internet training data becomes depleted. New research suggests that current data stocks may last longer than previously expected. Epoch AI estimates the total effective stock of data available for training models by token count as follows: Common Crawl contains a median of 130 trillion tokens, the indexed web holds approximately 510 trillion tokens, and the entire web (including private data) contains around 3,100 trillion tokens. Additionally, the stock of images is estimated at 300 trillion and video at 1,350 trillion. Epoch AI projects, with an 80% confidence interval, that the current stock of training data will be fully utilized between 2026 and 2032. This timeline is influenced by the historical growth of dataset sizes and computer usage. If models are trained in a compute-optimal manner, the data stock lasts longer; however, if models are overtrained—trained beyond the point of diminishing returns to achieve more compute-efficient inference—the stock may be depleted more quickly.

These projections revise earlier estimates from Epoch AI, which predicted high-quality text data would be depleted by 2024. The update reflects research showing that web data performs better than curated corpora and that models can be trained on the same datasets multiple times. While using synthetic data (data generated by AI models) as a solution to data shortages has been suggested, the 2024 AI Index suggests that models trained on repeated cycles of synthetic data likely lose representation of the tails of distributions, leading to degraded output quality (model collapse). However, when synthetic data is layered on top of real data rather than replacing it, the collapse phenomenon does not occur, although it does not necessarily improve performance or reduce test loss. 

Advances have been made in generating high-fidelity synthetic data, though it remains generally distinguishable from real data. A team of Slovenian researchers found that most synthetic relational data methods are detectable and typically deteriorate in performance compared to real data, though some methods like using Synthetic Data Vault (SDV) vs. Walmart data to train an XGBoost classifier showed synthetic data could outperform real data in some cases. In the healthcare domain, some model architectures using synthetic data have shown enhanced performance, increasing F1 scores or AUROC by 5%–10% on minority classes. To improve factuality, researchers from Stanford and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill introduced FactTune-FS methods, which have tended to outperform other RLHF and decoding-based methods. 

As web content becomes increasingly AI-generated, future models will inevitably be trained on non-human material. While synthetic data and data augmentation (modifying real data through tilting or image mixing) offer a near-infinite supply, their effective use requires further research into learning dynamics.

In terms of inference costs—the expense of querying a trained model, typically measured in USD per million tokens—the AI Index, working with Epoch AI, found that costs for a fixed AI performance threshold have decreased substantially. For an AI model scoring the equivalent of GPT-3.5 (64.8 on MMLU), the cost dropped from $20 per million tokens in November 2022 to $0.07 per million tokens by October 2024 (Gemini-1.5-Flash-8B), a more than 280-fold reduction. For models scoring above 50% on GPQA, costs declined from $15 per million tokens in May 2024 to $0.12 per million tokens by December 2024 (Phi 4). Epoch AI estimates that LLM inference costs have fallen between nine and 900 times per year depending on the task. While top-tier models from developers such as OpenAI, Meta, and Anthropic remain more expensive than smaller models, reflecting a premium for cutting-edge performance, the general trend shows AI performance per dollar has improved substantially.
chunk-009.summary: The 2025 AI Index Report notes that training compute for Chinese models has scaled 3x per year since 2021, while the US leads in compute intensity. It also projects that public training data may be depleted between 2026 and 2032, with a discussion on the risks and benefits of synthetic data and a 280-fold reduction in MMLU-equivalent inference costs from 2022 to 2024.

chunk-010.context:
The Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, provides detailed analysis on the training costs and hardware requirements of notable AI models. 

Regarding training costs, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman indicated that training GPT-4 exceeded $100 million, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei noted in July 2024 that model training runs costing around $1 billion were already underway. In contrast, more recent models such as DeepSeek-V3 reportedly cost less, approximately $6 million, although some reports dispute this figure, arguing that actual development costs were significantly higher when factoring in employee salaries, capital expenditures, and research expenses. To refine these estimates, the AI Index partnered with Epoch AI, which analyzed factors such as training duration, hardware type, quantity, and utilization rates using data from academic publications, press releases, and technical reports.

Epoch AI's estimates, based on cloud compute rental prices, show that training costs have significantly increased over time. For example, the original Transformer model (2017) cost approximately $670 to train, RoBERTa Large (2019) cost approximately $160,000, and OpenAI’s GPT-4 (2023) was estimated at around $79 million. For 2024 models, Llama 3.1-405B had an estimated training cost of $170 million. The AI Index notes a direct correlation between the training costs of AI models and their computational requirements, where models with greater computational needs cost substantially more to train.

Hardware advancements, particularly the development of more powerful and efficient GPUs (graphics processing units), have been critical in driving AI progress by accelerating complex computations and reducing training time. Using data from Epoch AI, the AI Index reports that machine learning hardware performance, measured in 16-bit floating-point operations, grew at an annual rate of approximately 43% between 2008 and 2024, doubling every 1.9 years. This progress is driven by increased transistor counts, semiconductor manufacturing advancements, and specialized AI hardware. Precision levels vary by use case: FP32 provides the highest precision for scientific computing, while lower-precision formats like Tensor-FP16/BF16 and FP16 are optimized for speed and energy efficiency, which is ideal for edge or mobile devices.

Specifically analyzing Nvidia data center GPUs, the H100 GPU (announced March 2022) achieves 22 billion FLOP per second per dollar, which is 1.7 times the price-performance of the A100 (June 2020) and 16.9 times that of the P100 (April 2016). Epoch AI estimates that the cost of hardware with a fixed performance level decreases by 30% annually. Regarding usage, the A100 was the most commonly reported hardware used to train notable AI models, used by 64 models, followed by the V100; however, 15 models were reported as trained on the H100 by the end of 2024.

Energy efficiency, measured in FLOP/s per watt, has also improved by approximately 40% per year. For example, the Nvidia B100 (March 2024) achieved an energy efficiency of 2.5 trillion FLOP/s per watt, making it 33.8 times more energy efficient than the Nvidia P100 (April 2016), which reported 74 billion FLOP/s per watt. Despite these hardware efficiency gains, the overall power consumption required to train frontier AI models is doubling annually because of the trend of training on larger datasets. For instance, the original Transformer (2017) consumed an estimated 4,500 watts, PaLM consumed 2.6 million watts, and Llama 3.1-405B (summer 2024) required 25.3 million watts—over 5,000 times the power of the original Transformer. This increase in power consumption has led to a corresponding rise in carbon emissions, influenced by factors such as model parameters, data center power usage effectiveness (PUE), and grid carbon intensity.
chunk-010.summary: Training costs for AI models have risen from $670 for the 2017 Transformer to $170 million for Llama 3.1-405B, while hardware performance grows 43% annually, with the Nvidia B100 being 33.8 times more energy efficient than the P100.

chunk-011.context:
The Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, reports that carbon emissions from training frontier AI models have steadily increased over time. While the emissions from training AlexNet (2012) were negligible (0.01 tons of CO2 equivalent), GPT-3 (released in 2020) reportedly emitted around 588 tons of carbon, GPT-4 (2023) emitted 5,184 tons, and Llama 3.1 405B (2024) emitted 8,930 tons. DeepSeek V3, released in 2024 and with performance comparable to OpenAI’s o1, is estimated to have carbon emissions comparable to GPT-3, which was released five years prior. For context, the average American emits 18.08 tons of carbon per capita per year.

To estimate these emissions, the AI Index used carbon data published by model developers and supplemented it with calculations from a widely used online AI training emissions calculator. This supplementation was necessary because many developers do not disclose their models’ carbon footprints. The calculator estimates emissions based on the type of hardware used for training, total training hours, cloud provider, and training region. The AI Index sourced input data—such as training hardware and duration—for the emissions calculator from various online sources and validated the accuracy of the calculator by comparing its estimates with actual emissions reported by developers, finding the results were largely consistent.

Additionally, the report provides data on other carbon-emitting activities: air travel for one passenger from New York to San Francisco emits 0.99 tons, the average human life emits 5.51 tons per year, and average car usage (including fuel) over a lifetime emits 63 tons.

Beyond environmental impact, the AI Index Report 2025 analyzes AI research and professional networking. AI conferences have expanded in scale, quantity, and prestige over the past two decades. Attendance at major AI conferences grew almost 21.7% from 2023 to 2024, with total attendees rising by more than 60,000 since 2014. Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) remains the most attended AI conference, attracting almost 20,000 participants in 2024. Other major conferences that saw attendance increases in the last year include CVPR, ICML, ICRA, ICLR, IROS, and AAAI. In 2021, a significant spike in ICML attendance was attributed to the conference being held virtually. Total attendance figures encompass virtual, hybrid, and in-person participation.

Furthermore, the report examines open-source AI software via GitHub data. Since 2011, the number of AI-related GitHub projects has consistently increased, growing from 1,549 in 2011 to approximately 4.3 million in 2024, with a sharp 40.3% rise in the last year alone. As of 2024, the United States accounts for 23.4% of GitHub AI project contributions, followed by India at 19.9% and Europe at 19.5%, though the U.S. share has declined since 2016. China accounts for 2.08% of contributions. The total number of new GitHub stars for AI-related projects rose from 14.0 million in 2023 to 17.7 million in 2024. In 2024, the United States led in cumulative GitHub stars with 21.08 million, followed by the 'Rest of the world' (16.39 million), Europe (10.29 million), India (4.06 million), and China (3.67 million). Popular libraries such as TensorFlow, Keras, PyTorch, and OpenCV are among the most starred repositories.
chunk-011.summary: Training emissions for frontier AI models rose from 0.01 tons for AlexNet to 8,930 tons for Llama 3.1 405B, while AI-related GitHub projects grew to 4.3 million by 2024 and NeurIPS became the most attended AI conference with nearly 20,000 participants.

reasoning, computer vision, speech, and agentic AI. New this year are significantly

benchmarks, including MMMU, GPQA, and SWE-bench, aimed at testing the limits of increasingly capable AI systems. By 2024,
AI performance on these benchmarks saw remarkable improvements, with gains of 18.8 and 48.9 percentage points on MMMU
and GPQA, respectively. On SWE-bench, AI systems could solve just 4.4% of coding problems in 2023—a figure that jumped
to 71.7% in 2024.

2. Open-weight models catch up. Last year’s AI Index revealed that leading open-weight models lagged significantly
behind their closed-weight counterparts. By 2024, this gap had nearly disappeared. In early January 2024, the leading closedweight model outperformed the top open-weight model by 8.04% on the Chatbot Arena Leaderboard. By February 2025, this
gap had narrowed to 1.70%.

3. The gap between Chinese and US models closes. In 2023, leading American models significantly outperformed
their Chinese counterparts—a trend that no longer holds. At the end of 2023, performance gaps on benchmarks such as MMLU,
MMMU, MATH, and HumanEval were 17.5, 13.5, 24.3, and 31.6 percentage points, respectively. By the end of 2024, these
differences had narrowed substantially to just 0.3, 8.1, 1.6, and 3.7 percentage points.

4. AI model performance converges at the frontier. According to last year’s AI Index, the Elo score difference between
the top and 10th-ranked model on the Chatbot Arena Leaderboard was 11.9%. By early 2025, this gap had narrowed to just
5.4%. Likewise, the difference between the top two models shrank from 4.9% in 2023 to just 0.7% in 2024. The AI landscape is
becoming increasingly competitive, with high-quality models now available from a growing number of developers.

5. New reasoning paradigms like test-time compute improve model performance. In 2024, OpenAI introduced
models like o1 and o3 that are designed to iteratively reason through their outputs. This test-time compute approach dramatically
improved performance, with o1 scoring 74.4% on an International Mathematical Olympiad qualifying exam, compared to GPT4o’s 9.3%. However, this enhanced reasoning comes at a cost: o1 is nearly six times more expensive and 30 times slower than
GPT-4o.

Technical Performance

Chapter Highlights (cont’d)
6. More challenging benchmarks are continually proposed. The saturation of traditional AI benchmarks like MMLU,
GSM8K, and HumanEval, coupled with improved performance on newer, more challenging benchmarks such as MMMU and
GPQA, has pushed researchers to explore additional evaluation methods for leading AI systems. Notable among these are
Humanity’s Last Exam, a rigorous academic test where the top system scores just 8.80%; FrontierMath, a complex mathematics
benchmark where AI systems solve only 2% of problems; and BigCodeBench, a coding benchmark where AI systems achieve a
35.5% success rate—well below the human standard of 97%.

7. High-quality AI video generators demonstrate significant improvement. In 2024, several advanced AI models
capable of generating high-quality videos from text inputs were launched. Notable releases include OpenAI’s SORA, Stable
Video 3D and 4D, Meta’s Movie Gen, and Google DeepMind’s Veo 2. These models produce videos of significantly higher quality
compared to those from 2023.

8. Smaller models drive stronger performance. In 2022, the smallest model registering a score higher than 60% on
MMLU was PaLM, with 540 billion parameters. By 2024, Microsoft’s Phi-3-mini, with just 3.8 billion parameters, achieved the
same threshold. This represents a 142-fold reduction in over two years.

9. Complex reasoning remains a problem. Even though the addition of mechanisms such as chain-of-thought
reasoning has significantly improved the performance of LLMs, these systems still cannot reliably solve problems for which
provably correct solutions can be found using logical reasoning, such as arithmetic and planning, especially on instances larger
than those they were trained on. This has a significant impact on the trustworthiness of these systems and their suitability in
high-risk applications.

10. AI agents show early promise. The launch of RE-Bench in 2024 introduced a rigorous benchmark for evaluating
complex tasks for AI agents. In short time-horizon settings (two-hour budget), top AI systems score four times higher than human
experts, but as the time budget increases, human performance surpasses AI—outscoring it two to one at 32 hours. AI agents
already match human expertise in select tasks, such as writing Triton kernels, while delivering results faster and at lower costs.

The Technical Performance chapter of the Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, provides a comprehensive overview of AI technical performance and significant model releases in 2024. 

### Significant Model and Dataset Releases of 2024
As selected by the AI Index Steering Committee, the following were some of the most notable AI releases in 2024:

*   **January 19, 2024 - Stable LM 2 (LLM, Stability AI):** An enhanced version of the original Stable LM with 1.6 billion parameters, designed for efficient operation on portable devices like smartphones and laptops.
*   **February 8, 2024 - Aya Dataset (Dataset, Cohere for AI, Beijing Academy of AI, Cohere, Binghamton University):** A collection of 513 million prompt-completion pairs across 114 languages, representing a milestone in multilingual instruction tuning.
*   **February 15, 2024 - Gemini 1.5 Pro (LLM, Google DeepMind):** This model established a new benchmark with a 1 million token context window, significantly exceeding the 128K token limit of GPT-4 Turbo.
*   **February 20, 2024 - SDXL-Lightning (Text-to-image, ByteDance):** A fast text-to-image system that generates high-quality synthetic images in under a second using progressive adversarial distillation rather than diffusion-based techniques.
*   **March 4, 2024 - Claude 3 (LLM, Anthropic):** An LLM that outperforms GPT-4 and Gemini on nearly all industry benchmarks while reducing incorrect prompt refusals and increasing accuracy.
*   **March 7, 2024 - Inflection-2.5 (LLM, Inflection AI):** A model with GPT-4-level performance that uses only 40% of the computing resources of GPT-4. Microsoft acquired Inflection for $650 million two weeks after the model's release.
*   **March 19, 2024 - Moirai and LOTSA (Model/Dataset, Salesforce):** Moirai is a foundation model for universal forecasting, and LOTSA is a large-scale time series dataset containing 27 billion observations across nine domains.
*   **March 27, 2024 - DBRX (LLM, Databricks):** An open-source mixture-of-experts (MoE) transformer decoder-only model with 132B parameters (36B active per input), trained on 12 trillion tokens, surpassing similar small MoE models like Mixtral and Grok.
*   **April 2, 2024 - Stable Audio 2 (Text-to-song and song-to-song, Stability AI):** A song generator that supports audio-to-audio functionality, allowing users to manipulate songs via natural language prompts.
*   **April 17, 2024 - Llama 3 (LLM, Meta):** A series of text-based models with 8B and 70B parameters, ranking among the highest performing models of their size.
*   **May 13, 2024 - GPT-4o (Multimodal, OpenAI):** A multimodal model that processes and generates text, audio, images, and video; it can respond to audio in as little as 320 milliseconds.
*   **June 7, 2024 - Qwen2 (LLM, Alibaba):** A series of base and instruction-tuned models that rival Llama 3-70B and Mixtral-8x22B in performance.
*   **June 17, 2024 - Runway Gen-3 (Text-to-video and image-to-video, Runway):** A video generation model that excels in creating photorealistic humans with vivid emotionality.
*   **July 23, 2024 - Llama 3.1 405B (LLM, Meta):** Meta's largest model with 405B parameters, which became the most capable openly available foundation model, rivaling many closed models.
*   **August 12, 2024 - Falcon Mamba (LLM, Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi):** A 7B parameter model based on the Mamba State Space Language Model (SSLM) architecture, which is more efficient than transformer-based models by dynamically adjusting parameters.
*   **August 13, 2024 - Grok-2 (Text-to-text and text-to-image, xAI):** An advanced reasoning and problem-solving model that rivaled leading models shortly after xAI was founded in March 2023.
*   **August 15, 2024 - Imagen 3 (Text-to-image, Google Labs):** An image generator that achieved the highest Elo score on the GenAI-Bench image benchmark.
*   **August 22, 2024 - Jamba 1.5 (LLM, AI21 Labs):** The first LLM to combine state-space models with transformers to enhance speed while preserving quality.
*   **August 29, 2024 - SynthID v2 (Tool, Google):** A watermarking and identification software supporting AI-generated images, video, audio, and text.
*   **September 11, 2024 - NotebookLM Podcast Tool (Text-to-podcast, Google Labs):** An end-to-end AI podcast generator used for study and summary purposes.
*   **September 12, 2024 - o1-preview (Language, math, biology, OpenAI):** The first in the "o series" designed for advanced reasoning, proving significantly more powerful than GPT in math, science, and coding.
*   **September 17, 2024 - NVLM (D, H, X) (Vision, language, Nvidia):** Three open-access models for vision-language tasks that achieved top scores on VQAv2 and OCRBench.
*   **September 19, 2024 - Qwen2.5 (LLM, Alibaba):** A series of foundation models including efficient smaller models and specialized coding and math models.
*   **October 16, 2024 - Ministral (LLM, Mistral):** A pair of compact models (3B and 8B parameters) that outperformed Gemma and Llama models of similar size.
*   **October 22, 2024 - Anthropic Computer Use (Agentic Capability, Anthropic):** A feature for Claude 3.5 Sonnet allowing the model to autonomously move the cursor and type on a user's computer in real time.
*   **October 28, 2024 - Apple Intelligence (iPhone feature, Apple):** A suite of AI features including Image Playground, Genmoji, and Siri integration with ChatGPT.
*   **December 3, 2024 - Nova Pro (Multimodal, Amazon):** The most powerful model in AWS's Nova family, specializing in the analysis of financial documents.
*   **December 11, 2024 - Gemini 2 (LLM, Google DeepMind):** An improved version of Gemini that is twice as fast as Gemini 1.5 Pro and includes computer control and image/audio generation.
*   **December 12, 2024 - Sora (Text-to-video, OpenAI):** A video generation model capable of creating 1080p videos up to 20 seconds long (for ChatGPT Pro users) and 720p videos up to five seconds long (for ChatGPT Plus users).
*   **December 13, 2024 - Global MMLU (Dataset, Cohere):** A multilingual evaluation set with professionally translated MMLU questions across 42 languages to reduce Western bias.
*   **December 20, 2024 - o3 (beta) (Multimodal, OpenAI):** A frontier model that outperforms previous models in PhD-level science, research math, competition math, and SWE, achieving a record 87.5% on the ARC-AGI private holdout set.
*   **December 27, 2024 - DeepSeek-V3 (LLM, DeepSeek):** An open-source model developed with fewer computing resources that outperforms leading models on GPQA and MMLU benchmarks.

### State of AI Performance
AI systems have continued to improve in 2024, exceeding human performance on several previously challenging benchmarks. 

In areas where human ability still surpasses AI, the gap is shrinking rapidly. For instance, on the MATH benchmark for competition-level mathematics, state-of-the-art AI systems are now 7.9 percentage points ahead of human performance, compared to a 0.3-point gap in 2024. On the MMMU benchmark for complex, multidisciplinary expert-level questions, the best 2024 model, o1, scored 78.2%, which is only 4.4 percentage points below the human benchmark of 82.6%.

Additionally, there is a narrowing gap between closed-weight and open-weight LLMs. According to the Chatbot Arena Leaderboard, the leading closed-weight model outperformed the top open-weight model by 8.0% in early January 2024; by February 2025, this gap had narrowed to 1.7%.

chunk-014.context:
The Technical Performance chapter of the Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, analyzes the performance gap between closed-weight and open-weight AI models. In 2023, closed-weight models consistently outperformed open-weight counterparts on nearly every major benchmark, including MMLU, HumanEval, MMMU, and MATH. By 2024, however, this gap narrowed significantly. For example, in late 2023, closed-weight models led open models on MMLU by 15.9 percentage points, but by the end of 2024, this difference shrunk to 0.1 percentage point. This rapid improvement in open-weight performance was largely driven by Meta's summer release of Llama 3.1, followed by other high-performing open-weight models such as DeepSeek's V3. Similarly, on the LMSYS Chatbot Arena, the leading closed-weight model outperformed the top open-weight model by 8.0% in early January 2024, narrowing to a 1.7% gap by February 2025.

AI models are released with different levels of openness. Some models, such as Google's Med-Gemini, remain entirely closed and accessible only to their developers. Others, like OpenAI's GPT-4o and Anthropic's Claude 3.5, provide limited public access through APIs, but their weights are not released, preventing independent modification or public scrutiny. In contrast, weights for Meta's Llama 3.3 and Stable Video 4D are fully available, allowing anyone to modify and use them freely. The AI Index notes that while open-weight models are more accessible than closed-weight models, they are not necessarily fully 'open source' because the underlying code or training data is often withheld. Perspectives on this divide are split: advocates argue open-weight models reduce monopolies, spur innovation, and improve transparency, citing the use of Meta's Llama models in creating tools like Meditron and powering military applications. Critics, however, warn that open-weight models pose security risks, including the potential for creating bioweapons or spreading disinformation.

Furthermore, the report examines the technical performance gap between the United States and China. Historically, the U.S. has dominated AI research and model development, but China-based models are rapidly catching up. In January 2024, the top U.S. model outperformed the best Chinese model by 9.3% on the LMSYS Chatbot Arena, but by February 2025, this gap narrowed to 1.7%. At the end of 2023, performance gaps between U.S. and Chinese models on the MMLU, MMMU, MATH, and HumanEval benchmarks were 17.5, 13.5, 24.3, and 31.6 percentage points, respectively. By the end of 2024, these differences narrowed to 0.3, 8.1, 1.6, and 3.7 percentage points. The launch of DeepSeek-R1 was particularly notable because the company reported achieving these results using only a fraction of the hardware resources typically required for such models, raising doubts about the effectiveness of U.S. semiconductor export controls.

Additionally, the report highlights the rise of smaller, high-performing AI models. While AI progress has traditionally been driven by scaling (increasing model size and data), 2024 saw a breakthrough in compact models, including GPT-4o mini, o1-mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Llama 3.1 8B, and Mistral Small 3.5. Smaller models are significant because they demonstrate increased algorithmic efficiency, lower training costs, and faster, less expensive inference. This trend is exemplified by the reduction in the size of the smallest model scoring above 60% on the MMLU benchmark: in 2022, the smallest such model was PaLM with 540 billion parameters, but by 2024, Microsoft's Phi-3 Mini achieved this threshold with only 3.8 billion parameters, a 142-fold reduction in size.

Finally, the report discusses the convergence of performance at the frontier. The AI landscape is becoming more competitive, with multiple providers now offering highly capable models. The Elo score difference between the top and 10th-ranked models on the Chatbot Arena Leaderboard narrowed from 11.9% (as reported in the previous AI Index) to 5.4% by early 2025. The difference between the top two models shrank from 4.9% in 2023 to 0.7% in 2024. Current top providers include Google, OpenAI, DeepSeek, xAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Mistral AI. The report also notes that many prominent AI benchmarks are reaching saturation, as AI systems advance so rapidly that new tests remain relevant for only a few years. To address this, the community is moving toward more rigorous evaluations, as some developers have used nonstandard prompting (such as Google's use of chain-of-thought prompting for Gemini Ultra's MMLU score) or reported results that perform worse in independent third-party testing.

chunk-015.context:
The Technical Performance chapter of the Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, discusses the complexities of benchmarking AI intelligence. While benchmarks are effective for evaluating discrete capabilities such as vision and language (e.g., classifying an image or answering a multiple-choice question), they are more challenging to develop for multi-agent systems and human-AI interaction due to the diversity of correct answers and variability in human behaviors.

AI advances have traditionally been measured through competitions like chess and poker, which involve human-to-machine challenges. A significant milestone in AI progress is the diminishing relevance of the Turing test, originally proposed in Alan Turing’s 1950 paper “Computing Machinery and Intelligence.” The Turing test evaluates a machine’s ability to exhibit humanlike intelligence via a text-based conversation with a human judge; if the judge cannot distinguish the machine from a human, the machine passes. Recent evidence suggests that modern Large Language Models (LLMs) have advanced to the point where people struggle to differentiate them from humans, signaling that these models can now pass the Turing test.

In robotics, new models have emerged that reason about natural laws and interact with the physical world. Benchmarks such as ARMBench focus on perception tasks, while VIMA-Bench assesses robot performance in simulated environments that incorporate deep learning, communication, and perception.

Benchmarks can suffer from several deficiencies. Some are poorly constructed; a study called BetterBench analyzed 24 prominent benchmarks and found that 14 failed to report statistical significance, 17 lacked scripts for result replication, and most had inadequate documentation. BetterBench proposed a 46-criteria framework for benchmark development (covering design, implementation, documentation, and maintenance) and a public repository to improve comparability. In Figure 2.1.41 of the report, MMLU demonstrated poor adherence to quality standards, whereas GPQA performed significantly better.

Additionally, benchmarks can suffer from contamination, where LLMs encounter test questions during their training. A study by Scale found significant contamination in the performance of many LLMs on the GSM8K mathematics benchmark. To combat this, researchers introduced LiveBench, which is periodically updated with new questions from unfamiliar sources to ensure models have not seen them during training.

Because benchmark scores influence policy and procurement decisions, the AI Index sources its data from company papers, blog posts, product releases, and public repositories like RankedAGI and Papers With Code. These scores are current as of mid-February 2025, though the report notes that newer models may have been released since then. The report also operates on the assumption that scores reported by companies are factual.

In the domain of Natural Language Processing (NLP), state-of-the-art models like OpenAI’s GPT-4o, Anthropic’s Claude 3.5, and Google’s Gemini can generate coherent prose and reason across audio, images, and goal-oriented tasks. A key benchmark for English language understanding is the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU), created in 2020 by researchers from UC Berkeley, Columbia University, University of Chicago, and University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. MMLU assesses zero-shot or few-shot performance across 57 subjects in STEM, humanities, and social sciences. OpenAI’s o1-preview achieved the highest recorded MMLU score of 92.3% in September 2024, compared to 86.4% for GPT-4 (March 2023) and 27.9% for RoBERTa in 2019, representing a 64.4 percentage point increase over five years. The human baseline for MMLU is 89.8%.

MMLU has been criticized for having overly simplistic or erroneous questions. Consequently, researchers from the University of Toronto, University of Waterloo, and Carnegie Mellon introduced MMLU-Pro in 2024, which removes trivial questions and increases answer choices. DeepSeek-R1 currently holds the highest score on MMLU-Pro at 84.0%. The report also warns that some developers use nonstandard prompting to boost MMLU scores and that reported scores can differ from academic evaluations by up to five percentage points.

For evaluating public preference, the LMSYS Chatbot Arena Leaderboard (launched in 2023) allows users to vote on anonymous model outputs. As of early 2025, the platform has over 1 million votes, with a Google Gemini model as the most preferred. The performance gap between the top model and the 10th-ranked model on the leaderboard narrowed from 11.9% (as reported in the 2024 AI Index) to 5.4% by early 2025.

To address the cost of human-curating benchmarks, UC Berkeley researchers created BenchBuilder, an automated pipeline that uses LLMs to curate open-ended prompts from crowdsourced data. The LMSYS team used BenchBuilder to develop Arena-Hard-Auto, which evaluates instruction-tuned LLMs using 500 challenging queries from the Chatbot Arena, with GPT-4 Turbo acting as the judge against a baseline model (GPT-4-0314). As of November 2024, the top scores on Arena-Hard-Auto were o1-mini (92.0), o1-preview (90.4), and Claude-3.5-Sonnet (85.2). However, the November variant of Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 3.5 is the top model on the style leaderboard, which accounts for how response style influences user preference.
chunk-015.summary: The AI Index Report 2025 details the evolution of AI benchmarking, noting that OpenAI's o1-preview reached a record 92.3% on MMLU while the gap between the top and 10th ranked models on the Chatbot Arena narrowed to 5.4%. It also highlights benchmark deficiencies, such as the contamination of GSM8K and the creation of MMLU-Pro to provide a more rigorous evaluation of LLMs.

chunk-016.context:
The Technical Performance chapter of the Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, discusses several new benchmarks and model capabilities in the domain of language.

Regarding the Arena-Hard-Auto benchmark, more than 50% of its questions focus specifically on coding and debugging. The benchmark also features a style control leaderboard to assess how response style influences preference. According to data from LMSYS (2025), models such as o1-mini (92.0), o1-preview (90.4), and Claude-3.5-Sonnet (85.2) achieved top scores on Arena-Hard-Auto. The November variant of Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 3.5 is the top model on the style leaderboard.

WildBench, developed in 2024 by researchers from the Allen Institute for AI and the University of Washington, evaluates Large Language Models (LLMs) on challenging, real-world queries. The creators of WildBench note that existing evaluations have limitations: MMLU focuses on academic questions and does not assess open-ended, real-world problems, while benchmarks like LMSYS rely heavily on human oversight and lack consistency in evaluating all models with the same dataset. WildBench addresses these issues by providing an automated evaluation framework using diverse "in the wild" questions selected from over 1 million human-chatbot interactions. Currently, GPT-4o is the top-performing model on WildBench with an Elo score of 1227.1, followed by Claude 3.5 Sonnet with a score of 1215.4.

OpenAI's latest models, o1 and o3, represent a paradigm shift in advanced reasoning through their use of a chain-of-thought process and the ability to iteratively check answers, a process known as inference or test-time computation. This allows the models to break complex problems into smaller steps before executing them. For instance, when deciphering scrambled text, o1 provides a more thorough reasoning process than GPT-4. 

Comparing benchmarks, o1 outperforms GPT-4o with a 2.8-point gain on MMLU, 34.5 points on MATH, 26.7 points on GPQA Diamond, and 65.1 points on AIME 2024. Specifically, o1 scored 74.4% on AIME 2024, compared to 9.3% for GPT-4o. In terms of machine intelligence, o3 achieved an 87.5% accuracy rate on the ARC-AGI benchmark, surpassing the previous record of 55.5%. However, these capabilities increase costs and latency. GPT-4o costs $2.50 per 1 million input tokens and $10 per 1 million output tokens, whereas o1 costs $15 per 1 million input tokens and $60 per 1 million output tokens. Furthermore, o1 is approximately 40 times slower than GPT-4o, with a time to first token of 29.7 seconds compared to 0.72 seconds for GPT-4o. OpenAI released o1-preview to ChatGPT Plus and Teams users on September 12, 2024, and released the full version of o1 and the $200 monthly ChatGPT Pro subscription on December 5, 2024. The o3 model is currently only available to select researchers and developers via OpenAI’s safety testing program.

MixEval, launched by researchers at the National University of Singapore, Carnegie Mellon University, and the Allen Institute for AI, is a benchmark that combines real-world user queries (similar to Chatbot Arena) with ground-truth-based questions (similar to MMLU). The MixEval-Hard suite focuses on substantially harder queries. On the MixEval-Hard benchmark, OpenAI’s o1-preview achieved the highest score of 72.0, followed by Claude 3.5 Sonnet-0620 (68.1) and Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct (66.2), all of which were released in 2024.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a capability where LLMs integrate with retrieval mechanisms to retrieve relevant information from documents before generating a response. In September 2024, Anthropic introduced Contextual Retrieval to enhance RAG capabilities. New benchmarks for RAG include Ragnarok and CRAG, as well as FinanceBench for financial question answering.

The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard evaluates the ability of LLMs to call functions or tools using over 2,000 question-function-answer pairs across languages like Python, Java, JavaScript, and REST API. The top model is watt-tool-70b (a fine-tuned variant of Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct), which achieved an overall accuracy of 74.31, followed by a November variant of GPT-4o with a score of 72.08. Top model accuracy on this benchmark improved by up to 50 points over the course of 2024.

Finally, the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB), created by Hugging Face and Cohere in late 2022, evaluates how models convert data into numerical embedding vectors to capture semantic meanings. MTEB includes 58 datasets spanning 112 languages and eight embedding tasks, such as bitext mining.
chunk-016.summary: The AI Index Report 2025 analyzes new language benchmarks including WildBench, MixEval, and the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard, while detailing OpenAI's o1 and o3 models' shift toward inference-time compute and the associated increases in latency and token costs.

chunk-017.context:
The Technical Performance chapter of the Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, provides an analysis of language embedding and long-context retrieval capabilities, as well as computer vision and image generation.

Regarding the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB), which was introduced in late 2022 and covers eight tasks (bitext mining, classification, clustering, pair classification, reranking, retrieval, semantic textual similarity, and summarization), the top-performing embedding model as of early 2025 was Voyage AI’s voyage-3-m-exp with a score of 74.03. This model, a variant of the voyage-3-large foundation model designed for embedding tasks, utilizes quantization-aware training and Matryoshka Representation Learning to improve performance. Voyage AI specializes in high-quality AI embedding models. The voyage-3-m-exp model narrowly outperformed NV-Embed-v2, which had a score of 72.31 and held the top spot for most of 2024. Since the introduction of MTEB in late 2022, when the leading model scored 59.5, average performance on the benchmark has meaningfully improved.

As the context windows of Large Language Models (LLMs) have expanded, evaluating long-context settings has become more critical. Early evaluations typically focused on "needle-in-the-haystack" scenarios, where models retrieve specific pieces of information from lengthy texts. However, more recent models, such as GPT-4o (May 2024) and Gemini 2.0 Pro Experimental (February 2025), now boast context windows ranging from 128 thousand to 2 million tokens. In contrast, 2023 models like GPT-4 and Llama 2, released by OpenAI and Meta respectively, featured windows of 8,000 and 4,000 tokens. 

To address limitations in long-context assessments, several new evaluation suites were introduced in 2024. Nvidia’s RULER benchmark assesses long-context performance through multihop reasoning, aggregation, retrieval performance, and question answering. On RULER, Gemini-1.5-Pro achieved the highest weighted performance average of 95.5, followed by GPT-4 (89.0) and GLM4 (88.0). The RULER team also found that while most popular LLMs claim context sizes of 32K tokens or greater, only half can maintain satisfactory performance at that length, meaning actual operational context windows are often shorter than claimed.

Another long-context evaluation benchmark introduced in 2024 is HELMET (How to Evaluate Long-Context Models Effectively and Thoroughly), a collaboration between Intel and Princeton. HELMET features seven evaluation categories, including passage re-ranking and synthetic recall. On the HELMET benchmark across 8K, 32K, and 128K context settings, models such as Gemini 1.5 Pro and the August variant of GPT-4 maintained their effectiveness, while GPT-4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Llama 3.1-70B showed performance degradation in longer settings.

In the domain of computer vision, vision models are evaluated on their ability to understand images and videos. While ImageNet was a foundational benchmark for straightforward tasks like image classification, modern benchmarks focus on more complex, open-ended challenges. The Visual Commonsense Reasoning (VCR) challenge, introduced in 2019 by the University of Washington and the Allen Institute for AI, tests the ability of AI systems to answer questions and provide the rationale behind those answers, measured by the Q->AR score. In July 2024, a model reached a Q->AR score of 85.0, matching the human benchmark and representing a 4.2% improvement over 2023.

For video understanding, the MVBench benchmark, introduced in 2023 by researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shanghai AI Laboratory, the University of Hong Kong, Fudan University, and Nanjing University, requires temporal reasoning across multiple frames. As of 2024, the top model on MVBench is Video-CCAM-7B-v1.2 (built on the Qwen 2.5-7B-Instruct language model) with a score of 69.23, a 14.6% improvement since the benchmark's introduction in late 2023.

Regarding image generation, the report notes that AI-generated images of human faces are now frequently indistinguishable from real photos. Midjourney's progress is exemplified by its evolution from 2022 to 2025; while its 2022 models produced cartoonish renderings of "a hyper-realistic image of Harry Potter," the 2025 versions create startlingly realistic depictions.
chunk-017.summary: Voyage AI's voyage-3-m-exp leads the MTEB benchmark with a score of 74.03, while Gemini-1.5-Pro tops the RULER long-context benchmark with a score of 95.5. AI has matched the human baseline of 85.0 on the Visual Commonsense Reasoning (VCR) benchmark and improved 14.6% on the MVBench video understanding benchmark.

chunk-018.context:
The AI community has increasingly used public evaluation platforms like the Chatbot Arena Leaderboard to assess the capabilities of leading AI systems, including top AI image generators. The Chatbot Arena Leaderboard features a Vision Arena that ranks the performance of over 50 vision models. In this arena, users submit text-to-image prompts—for example, "Batman drinking a coffee"—and vote for their preferred generation. To date, the Vision Arena has gathered more than 150,000 votes. As of early 2025, the top-ranked vision model on the Chatbot Arena leaderboard is Google’s Gemini-2.0-Flash-Thinking-Exp-1219. Performance among leading models is closely clustered; for instance, the gap between the top-ranked model and the fourth-ranked model, ChatGPT-4o-latest (2024-1120), is only 3.4%.

Regarding video generation, recent years have seen the rise of models capable of creating videos from text prompts. While earlier models had limitations such as low quality, lack of sound, or very short clips, 2024 marked a significant leap forward. In November 2023, Stability AI launched Stable Video Diffusion, its first foundation model for high-quality video generation. In March 2024, Stability AI introduced Stable Video 3D, which generates multiple 3D views and videos of an object from a single image. In February 2024, OpenAI previewed Sora, a diffusion model that creates a base video and refines it by removing noise over multiple steps; Sora became publicly accessible in December 2024 and can generate 20-second videos at resolutions up to 1080p. In October 2024, Meta unveiled the latest version of Movie Gen, which includes personalized video generation from images, high-quality video editing based on instructions, and the ability to incorporate sound; Movie Gen can create 16-second videos at 1080p resolution and 16 frames per second. Google also launched two video generation models: Veo in May 2024 and Veo 2 in December 2024. Internal benchmarking by Google showed that Veo 2 outperformed other leading generators including Meta’s Movie Gen, Kling v1.5, and Sora Turbo, with users consistently favoring Veo 2 in comparisons. Other notable contributions include Runway’s Gen-3 Alpha, Luma’s Dream Machine, and Kuaishou’s Kling 1.5. Progress is illustrated by the "Will Smith eating spaghetti" prompt, where videos generated by the generator Pika in 2025 show dramatic quality improvements over those produced in 2023.

In the domain of speech, AI systems can transcribe spoken words to text and recognize individual speakers. Speech recognition, the ability to convert spoken words into text, is evaluated on the LRS2 (Oxford-BBC Lip Reading Sentences 2) benchmark, introduced in 2017, which uses audio-visual clips from talk shows and news programs. Performance is measured by Word Error Rate (WER), where lower scores indicate higher precision. The model Whisper-Flamingo set a new standard on the LRS2 benchmark with a WER of 1.3%, surpassing the 2023 state-of-the-art score. However, the AI Index Report 2025 suggests this benchmark may be nearing saturation.

In the domain of coding, Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as assistants. Because foundational benchmarks like HumanEval—which uses 164 handwritten programming problems—are becoming saturated (with Claude 3.5 Sonnet (HPT) achieving a score of 100%), researchers are moving toward more complex challenges. SWE-bench, introduced in October 2023 by Princeton and University of Chicago researchers, uses 2,294 software engineering problems from GitHub and Python repositories. On the SWE-bench Verified subset, the best performing model at the end of 2023 scored 4.4%, but by early 2025, OpenAI’s o3 model solved 71.7% of the problems. To address the need for tests that require invoking diverse functions across libraries, an international team released BigCodeBench in 2024. BigCodeBench consists of 1,140 tasks across 139 libraries and seven domains. On the hard subset of BigCodeBench (specifically the "complete" and "instruct" tasks), the best model, OpenAI’s o1, achieved an average score of 35.5. On the Chatbot Arena LLM leaderboard's coding filter, the top model is Gemini-Exp-1206 with a score of 1,369, followed by OpenAI’s o1 at 1,361.
chunk-018.summary: The AI Index Report 2025 details advancements in vision and video generation, noting Google's Gemini-2.0-Flash-Thinking-Exp-1219 leads the Vision Arena and Veo 2 outperforms competitors. It also records Whisper-Flamingo's 1.3% WER on the LRS2 speech benchmark and OpenAI's o3 solving 71.7% of SWE-bench Verified problems.

chunk-019.context:
The Technical Performance chapter of the Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, provides data on AI model performance across coding, mathematics, and reasoning. In the domain of coding, the LMSYS Chatbot Arena for LLMs coding filter shows that among Chinese models, DeepSeek-V3 leads with an Elo score of 1,317, which trails the highest-ranking model by 3.8%.

Regarding mathematical problem-solving, benchmarks evaluate an AI system's ability to reason mathematically across levels ranging from grade-school to competition-standard mathematics. The GSM8K benchmark, introduced by OpenAI in 2021, consists of approximately 8,000 diverse grade-school math word problems requiring multistep arithmetic solutions. The top-performing model on GSM8K is a variant of Claude Sonnet 3.5 optimized using the HPT prompting strategy, which achieved a score of 97.72%, a significant increase from the 2023 high of 91.00%. However, in 2024, several models from Mistral, Meta, and Qwen scored around 96%, suggesting the GSM8K benchmark may be approaching saturation.

For more challenging tasks, the MATH dataset, introduced in 2021 by UC Berkeley and University of Chicago researchers, contains 12,500 competition-level mathematics problems. While AI systems initially solved only 6.9% of these problems, OpenAI’s o3-mini (high) model achieved a record score of 97.9% in January 2025, surpassing the human baseline of 90%.

Public preference in mathematics is tracked via the Chatbot Arena's math filter, which has collected over 340,000 public votes across 181 models. Unlike the general and coding arenas where Gemini-based models lead, the top-ranked model in the Math Arena is an OpenAI o1 variant released in December 2024.

To address the saturation of high school and college-level benchmarks, Epoch AI introduced FrontierMath, a benchmark featuring hundreds of original, exceptionally challenging problems in areas such as number theory, real analysis, algebraic geometry, and category theory. When first released, the best-performing model, Gemini 1.5 Pro, solved only 2.0% of the problems, while other leading models including o1-preview, o1-mini, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Grok 2 Beta also showed very low success rates. However, OpenAI’s o3 model is reported to have scored 25.2% on FrontierMath.

In the area of theorem proving, Google DeepMind developed AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry 2 for the 2024 International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO). AlphaProof, a reinforcement learning system derived from AlphaZero, uses a fine-tuned Gemini model to translate natural language problems into the Lean formal proof system. AlphaGeometry 2 is a neuro-symbolic hybrid system using a Gemini-based language model trained on synthetic data. Together, they solved four out of six problems in the 2024 IMO: AlphaProof solved two algebra problems and one number theory problem, while AlphaGeometry 2 solved the sole geometry problem in 24 seconds. This achieved a performance level equivalent to an IMO silver medalist, who typically solves 22.9 geometry problems in the IMO-AG-30 benchmarking set, whereas AlphaGeometry solved 25 out of 30 problems.

Finally, the report discusses general reasoning. As older benchmarks like SQuAD and VQA have become saturated, researchers from the United States and Canada developed the Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark (MMMU). MMMU contains approximately 11,500 college-level questions across six core disciplines: art and design, business, science, health and medicine, humanities and social science, and technology and engineering. As of January 2025, OpenAI’s o1 is the highest-performing model on MMMU with a score of 78.2%, improving upon the state-of-the-art score of 59.4% reported in the 2024 AI Index, though it remains below the human expert baseline of 82.6%.
chunk-019.summary: AI performance in mathematics has reached a milestone with OpenAI's o3-mini solving 97.9% of MATH problems, surpassing the 90% human baseline, while the o3 model scored 25.2% on the advanced FrontierMath benchmark.

chunk-020.context:
The Technical Performance chapter of the Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, analyzes advancements in AI reasoning and agentic capabilities.

Regarding general, multisubject AI reasoning, researchers from NYU, Anthropic, and Meta introduced the GPQA benchmark to test AI systems. The GPQA dataset consists of 448 difficult multiple-choice questions crafted by subject-matter experts in fields such as biology, physics, and chemistry, designed to be resistant to simple web searches. In the 2023 AI Index, the best-performing model, GPT-4, achieved a score of 38.8% on the GPQA diamond test set (the most challenging subset and the one most frequently tested by AI developers). By December 2024, OpenAI's o3 model achieved a state-of-the-art score of 87.7% on the diamond set, a 48.9 percentage point improvement over the 2023 state-of-the-art. OpenAI's o3 was the first model to exceed the baseline accuracy of 81.3% set by expert human validators.

To evaluate the ability of AI systems to generalize beyond prior training, François Chollet (creator of the Keras deep learning library) introduced the ARC-AGI benchmark in 2019. ARC-AGI presents AI systems with independent tasks featuring demonstration or input pairs followed by test or output scenarios, requiring assumed prior knowledge (such as basic topology, objects, and elementary arithmetic) rather than specialized world knowledge. In 2020, the top-performing system on ARC-AGI scored 20%, and by 2024, the score rose to 33%. However, OpenAI's o3 model achieved a score of 75.7%. When o3 was allocated a high compute budget exceeding the benchmark's $10,000 limit, it reached a score of 87.5%. Researchers suggest that previous slow progress was due to an overemphasis on scaling model size and training data, whereas recent gains indicate a shift toward improving search capabilities and generalization.

Due to the saturation of benchmarks like MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval, the team behind MMLU introduced Humanity's Last Exam (HLE), a benchmark comprising 2,700 highly challenging multimodal questions across dozens of subject areas. These questions were contributed by leading professors and graduate-level reviewers and were specifically tested against state-of-the-art LLMs before inclusion to ensure no existing model could answer them. Initial testing shows HLE is extremely difficult; for example, OpenAI's o1 scores only 8.8%, while other models such as Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking (7.2%), Gemini 1.5 Pro (5.2%), Claude 3.5 Sonnet (4.8%), Grok-2 (3.9%), and GPT-4o (3.1%) score even lower. Researchers speculate performance could exceed 50% by the end of 2025.

In the domain of planning—reasoning about actions that alter the world—Arizona State University proposed PlanBench, a suite of 600 problems based on the International Planning Competition. PlanBench tests models on tasks such as constructing stacks of blocks (Blocksworld), where a hand can only move one block at a time. In the Blocksworld zero-shot evaluation, OpenAI's o1 scored 97.8%, significantly outperforming Llama 3.1 405B (62.6%) and GPT-4o (35.5%). In the more difficult Mystery Blocksworld domain, where answers are syntactically obfuscated, o1 scored 52.8%, while Llama 3.1 405B scored 0.8% and GPT-4 scored 0%. Despite these gains, o1 solves only 23.6% of planning instances that require at least 20 steps.

Additionally, the report discusses AI agents—autonomous or semiautonomous systems designed to accomplish goals in specific environments. Because agentic tasks are diverse and dynamic, they are harder to benchmark than image classification. In 2024, VisualAgentBench (VAB) was launched to test agents in three categories: embodied agents (household and gaming), GUI agents (mobile and web apps), and visual design agents (CSS debugging). On the VAB test set, GPT-4o achieved the highest overall success rate at 36.2%, while most proprietary models averaged around 20%.

To test the R&D capabilities of AI systems, researchers launched RE-Bench in 2024, featuring seven open-ended machine learning research environments, such as optimizing a kernel or fine-tuning GPT-2. In short time-horizon settings (two-hour budget), the best AI systems score four times higher than human experts. However, in a 32-hour budget setting, humans outperform AI by a factor of two. Some tasks, such as writing custom Triton kernels, can be completed by AI agents more quickly than by any human expert.
chunk-020.summary: OpenAI's o3 model set new records on the GPQA diamond set (87.7%) and ARC-AGI (75.7%-87.5%), while AI agents showed strength in short-term tasks on RE-Bench but were outperformed by humans in 32-hour budget settings.

chunk-021.context:
The Technical Performance chapter of the Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, details several benchmarks and advancements in AI reasoning, robotics, and autonomous vehicles.

Regarding general AI assistants, Meta introduced the GAIA benchmark in May 2024. GAIA consists of 466 questions designed to assess the ability of AI systems to perform a broad range of tasks, including reasoning, multimodal processing, web browsing, and tool use. Unlike exam-style questions, GAIA challenges AI models with complex, multistep problems that may require searching the open web, interpreting multimodal inputs, and reasoning through intricate scenarios. When GAIA was launched, researchers found that existing Large Language Models (LLMs) lagged significantly behind human performance; for example, GPT-4 with plugins correctly answered only 15% of the questions, compared to 92% for human respondents. By 2024, the top system on GAIA achieved a score of 65.1%, which is a roughly 30 percentage point increase over the highest score recorded in 2023.

In the field of robotics, the Robot Learning Benchmark (RLBench), launched in 2019, is one of the most widely adopted benchmarks and features 100 unique tasks ranging from simple target reaching to opening an oven and placing a tray inside. Researchers typically evaluate systems on a standardized subset of 18 tasks. As of January 2025, the top-performing model on this subset is SAM2Act—a collaboration between the University of Washington, Universidad Católica San Pablo, Nvidia, and the Allen Institute for AI—which achieved an 86.8% success rate. This represents a 2.8 percentage point improvement over the 2024 state-of-the-art and a 66.7 percentage point increase from the leading score in 2021.

Humanoid robotics saw significant growth in 2024. Figure AI launched Figure 02, a general-purpose humanoid robot standing 5 feet 6 inches tall, weighing 154 pounds, and capable of handling a 44-pound payload. Figure 02 can operate for up to five hours on a single charge and can perform tasks such as making coffee and assisting in automotive assembly by placing sheet metal into a car fixture. Integrated with OpenAI, Figure 02 can engage in speech-to-speech reasoning to explain its actions and respond to queries. Other notable humanoid robots include Tesla’s Optimus (first launched in 2002 and redesigned in 2023) and Boston Dynamics’ Atlas.

Google DeepMind also made several robotic advancements. In 2023, DeepMind launched PaLM-E and RT-2, which used transformer-based architectures and training on both manipulation and language data to excel at both robotic manipulation and text generation. In 2024, DeepMind introduced AutoRT, an AI system that uses foundation models to autonomously generate training data by coordinating multiple video-equipped robots; AutoRT has generated a dataset of 77,000 robotic trials across 6,650 unique tasks. Additionally, DeepMind developed SARA-RT, which uses a technique called "up-training" to convert the quadratic complexity of standard transformers into a linear model, reducing computational demands while maintaining performance. DeepMind also developed the ALOHA (Autonomous and DemoStart Learning of High-level Activities) approach, enabling robots to perform intricate tasks such as tying shoelaces, hanging a shirt, and stacking kitchen items. DemoStart, another DeepMind method, is an auto-curriculum reinforcement learning method that allows robotic arms to master complex behaviors using sparse rewards and limited demonstrations. Furthermore, DeepMind introduced a robotic model in 2024 capable of reaching amateur human-level performance in competitive table tennis.

In 2024, there was a significant push toward robotic foundation models. Nvidia introduced GR00T (Generalist Robot 00 Technology), a general-purpose foundation model for humanoid robots designed to mimic human movements and understand natural language, along with data pipelines, simulation frameworks, and the Thor robotics computer. Other robotic foundation models include Covariant's RFM-1, which features language reasoning and real-world maneuverability, and LLaRA, developed by researchers at Stony Brook University and the University of Wisconsin-Madison, which integrates perception, communication, and action into a single deep learning model. These follow the 2023 trend of models like RT-2, PaLM-E, and Open-X Embodiment.

Regarding self-driving cars, Waymo (a subsidiary of Alphabet) operates robotaxis in Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Austin. As of January 2025, Waymo provides 150,000 paid rides per week, covering over a million miles. Waymo has driven the following rider-only miles through September 2024: 20.823 million in Phoenix, 10.209 million in San Francisco, 1.947 million in Los Angeles, and 124,000 in Austin. Waymo also plans to test vehicles in 10 additional cities, including Las Vegas, San Diego, and Miami, and has tested in snowy conditions in upstate New York and Truckee, California. In China, Baidu’s Apollo Go reported 988,000 rides in Q3 2024, a 20% year-over-year increase; as of October 2024, Apollo Go operated 400 robotaxis with plans to expand to 1,000 by the end of 2025. Pony.AI also plans to scale its fleet from 200 to between 2,000 and 3,000 vehicles by the end of 2026. China is currently testing more driverless cars than any other country and is rolling them out across 16 cities. In Europe, startups like Wayve are also gaining traction.

CHAPTER 3:
Responsible AI

Overview
Artificial intelligence is now deeply integrated into nearly every aspect of our lives. It
is reshaping sectors like education, finance, and healthcare, where algorithm-driven
insights guide critical decisions. While this shift offers significant benefits, it also brings
with it notable risks. The past year has seen a continued concentration of effort on the
responsible development and deployment of AI systems.
This chapter examines trends in responsible AI (RAI) across several dimensions. It
begins by establishing key RAI definitions before assessing broadly relevant issues
such as AI incidents, standardization challenges in LLM responsibility, and benchmarks
for model factuality and truthfulness. Next, it explores RAI trends within key societal
sectors—industry, academia, and policymaking—and analyzes specific subtopics,
including privacy and data governance, fairness, transparency and explainability,
and security and safety, using benchmarks that illuminate model performance and
highlights of notable research. The chapter concludes with a study of two special RAI
topics: agentic AI and election misinformation.

Table of Contents

Chapter 3 Preview

163

 Artificial Intelligence
Index Report 2025

CHAPTER 3:
Responsible AI

Chapter Highlights
1. Evaluating AI systems with responsible AI criteria is still uncommon, but new benchmarks are beginning
to emerge. Last year’s AI Index highlighted the lack of standardized RAI benchmarks for LLMs. While this issue persists, new
benchmarks such as HELM Safety and AIR-Bench help to fill this gap.

2. The number of AI incident reports continues to increase. According to the AI Incidents Database, the number of
reported AI-related incidents rose to 233 in 2024—a record high and a 56.4% increase over 2023.

3. Organizations acknowledge RAI risks, but mitigation efforts lag. A McKinsey survey on organizations’ RAI
engagement shows that while many identify key RAI risks, not all are taking active steps to address them. Risks including
inaccuracy, regulatory compliance, and cybersecurity were top of mind for leaders with only 64%, 63%, and 60% of respondents,
respectively, citing them as concerns.

4. Across the globe, policymakers demonstrate a significant interest in RAI. In 2024, global cooperation on AI
governance intensified, with a focus on articulating agreed-upon principles for responsible AI. Several major organizations—
including the OECD, European Union, United Nations, and African Union—published frameworks to articulate key RAI concerns
such as transparency and explainability, and trustworthiness.

5. The data commons is rapidly shrinking. AI models rely on massive amounts of publicly available web data for training.
A recent study found that data use restrictions increased significantly from 2023 to 2024, as many websites implemented new
protocols to curb data scraping for AI training. In actively maintained domains in the C4 common crawl dataset, the proportion
of restricted tokens jumped from 5–7% to 20–33%. This decline has consequences for data diversity, model alignment, and
scalability, and may also lead to new approaches to learning with data constraints.

6. Foundation model research transparency improves, yet more work remains. The updated Foundation
Model Transparency Index—a project tracking transparency in the foundation model ecosystem—revealed that the average
transparency score among major model developers increased from 37% in October 2023 to 58% in May 2024. While these gains
are promising, there is still considerable room for improvement.

Chapter Highlights (cont’d)
7. Better benchmarks for factuality and truthfulness. Earlier benchmarks like HaluEval and TruthfulQA, aimed at
evaluating the factuality and truthfulness of AI models, have failed to gain widespread adoption within the AI community. In
response, newer and more comprehensive evaluations have emerged, such as the updated Hughes Hallucination Evaluation

chunk-022.context:
The Technical Performance chapter of the Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, published by the AI Index Steering Committee at Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI, details advancements in autonomous motion and robotics. 

Regarding self-driving vehicles, Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in October 2024, a two-passenger autonomous vehicle without a steering wheel or pedals, expected to enter production in 2026 at a price under $30,000. Tesla also unveiled the Robovan, an electric autonomous van capable of transporting up to 20 passengers. In China, Baidu's Apollo Go launched the RT6 robotaxi, which features a battery-swapping system and a price tag of $30,000. Business partnerships have also expanded, such as Uber's collaboration with WeRide—the first publicly listed robotaxi company—to develop an autonomous ride-sharing platform in Abu Dhabi. 

In the realm of autonomous freight, companies like Kodiak have completed their first driverless deliveries. Aurora has reported over 1 million miles of autonomous freight hauling on U.S. highways since 2021, although these miles were completed with human safety drivers present. Aurora has also delayed the commercial launch of its fleet from the end of 2024 to April 2025.

To evaluate these capabilities, new benchmarks were introduced in 2024. NuPlan, developed by Motional, is a large-scale autonomous driving dataset and evaluation framework for testing machine-learning-based motion planners, featuring 1,282 hours of diverse driving scenarios and a training set of over 2 million fully annotated frames from more than 10,000 clips. Bench2Drive provides a comprehensive, realistic, closed-loop testing simulation environment for end-to-end autonomous vehicles to address the limitations of open-loop evaluations, which often lead to models that memorize patterns rather than learning to drive. According to the Bench2Drive benchmark, various autonomous driving methods achieved different driving scores, with top performers including TCP* (64.22), DriveAdapter (49.30), and ThinkTwice (40.73). Additionally, OpenAD is the first real-world, open-world autonomous driving benchmark for 3D object detection, focusing on domain generalization (the ability to adapt across diverse sensor configurations) and open-vocabulary recognition (the ability to identify previously unseen semantic categories).

Safety data suggests that self-driving cars may be safer than human drivers. Data for Waymo vehicles in Phoenix and San Francisco shows they have significantly fewer incidents per million miles than human benchmarks: 0.32 airbag deployments compared to 5.91 for humans, 0.90 injury-reported crashes compared to 4.06 for humans, and 1.74 police-reported incidents compared to 2.26 for humans. Waymo's performance shows a percentage difference to the human benchmark of -88% for airbag deployments in Phoenix and -87% in San Francisco, -78% for injury-reported crashes in Phoenix and -76% in San Francisco, and -77% for police-reported incidents in Phoenix and -88% in San Francisco.

Furthermore, a study conducted by Waymo and Swiss Re, a leading reinsurer, analyzed liability claims across 25.3 million miles driven. The study found that Waymo vehicles had an 88% reduction in property damage claims and a 92% reduction in bodily injury claims compared to human-driver baselines. In real terms, Waymo vehicles were involved in only nine property damage claims and two bodily injury claims over that distance, whereas human drivers would be expected to incur 78 property damage claims and 26 bodily injury claims.
